studies.title: A Man From Among Them
studies.meaning: Three disconnected letters open the surah, followed by a claim about the Book they head. Then comes a question about astonishment. The objection was never that God might speak, but that He spoke through a neighbour. Early scholars read the promise of a sure footing as reward already secured, as honest precedence with God, or as firm standing ahead of the believers. The charge of sorcery concedes the power of the words while refusing their source.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stage when the message had been public long enough for the city to settle into a position on it. Curiosity had hardened into accusation. This surah belongs to a small group that open with the same three letters and then speak immediately about scripture. Its audience knew the speaker personally, had traded with him, and had once trusted him with their deposits.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to restrain and to judge soundly. Applied to a book it carries both wisdom of content and tightness of construction, something whose parts hold and cannot be pulled loose.
Literally a foot of truthfulness. The classical range covers a reward already stored up, an honest standing with God, and firm ground underfoot. The image is of standing, not of receiving.
The accusation admits that the words worked. Sorcery was the available account of speech that moved crowds and divided households, and the same charge was thrown at earlier messengers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on reputation. A man's word was collateral on a caravan loan, and every household knew who honoured his and who did not. That is exactly where the objection landed: not on the content of the message but on the ordinariness of the man carrying it. Someone who had grown up in your alleys, whose uncles you could name, was the last person you expected speech from beyond to arrive through.
studies.didYouKnow: These three letters head exactly five surahs of the Quran: the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth and fifteenth. The thirteenth breaks the run by adding a fourth letter. In all five, the letters are followed at once by a statement about the Book. Nowhere in the text are the letters themselves explained.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The difficulty of revelation sits in the messenger, not in the message. God spoke through someone inside the community. So the words arrive with a life story attached. They can be argued with on those grounds. Asking for something grander is a request to be spared the work of weighing what was said. Note also that the good news comes before any argument.

crossReferences.why: States the objection directly: what stopped people believing was that God sent a human messenger.
The same complaint in detail, that this messenger eats food and walks through the markets.
Records both halves of the reaction here, astonishment at a warner from among them, then the charge of magic.

studies.applyIt: Notice today the moment you dismiss something true because of who said it. A colleague you find tiresome, a relative you filed away years ago. Try holding the sentence on its own for ten seconds before you attach it to the person. Familiarity did work in Mecca that argument could not, and it still does.
studies.explainEasier: People were surprised that God sent a message through an ordinary man they knew. He was told to warn them and to give good news to those who believe. Some just called him a magician.

studies.title: Governing All Things
studies.meaning: Four claims arrive in one sentence. God made the heavens and the earth over six days. He rose above the Throne. He runs the affair without pause. And He admits no one to speak up for another without His leave. The classical scholars take the settling over the Throne as stated, without asking how. They read the ongoing governing as an answer to a worry: that a creator might finish and withdraw. The conclusion drawn is worship, and the closing question asks only for thought.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience already accepted a supreme creator. What they argued about was whether He could be reached without go-betweens. Their shrine held images taken as advocates who could carry a request upward. Putting all speaking up for others under God's permission cuts at that arrangement. It does not deny that such speaking up happens. The surah comes back to this point several times before it ends.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars take the word as it stands without assigning it a manner, and warn against picturing a body seated. What it shows is completed sovereignty over creation rather than any location within it.
From a root meaning to consider the outcome of a matter. The form is continuous, so it describes ongoing management with an end in view, not a single act of setting things going.
One who joins his petition to another's, from a root meaning to make even-numbered. The word is not denied here; it is placed after permission, and that moves the whole transaction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in Mecca ran through patrons. A stranger entering the city sought protection from a man of standing before he could trade safely. A debtor in trouble looked for someone to speak for him to the creditor. Everyone knew that reaching a powerful man meant finding someone he already listened to. That habit was carried straight into worship. This ayah addresses it.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that God created the heavens and the earth in six days appears seven times in the Quran. In five of those places the settling over the Throne follows at once. The length of a day here is never defined. The classical scholars declined to fix it, noting only that the sun was not yet made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and government are held together. The world is not left running on its own. God's rule is described in a way that resists picturing, and the tradition guards that carefully. The biggest change is what happens to speaking up for someone before God. It is neither abolished nor made a lever. It is folded inside permission, so hope survives while the idea of pressuring God does not.

crossReferences.why: The same six days and Throne, expanded into night pursuing day and the stars under command.
Puts intercession under permission in the same terms, inside the best-known description of God.
Repeats the sequence and adds that apart from Him you have no master and no intercessor.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing today that is running without you: traffic lights, the person who restocks your shop, your own heartbeat. Follow it back a step or two and notice how little of it you arranged. The ayah does not ask you to feel small. It asks you to reflect, which is slower and more interesting.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth in six days. Then He rose above the Throne, and He runs everything all the time. No one can speak up for you with Him unless He allows it.

studies.title: He Begins It And Repeats It
studies.meaning: The argument for resurrection here is a comparison, not a threat. Whoever started a thing can start it again. The second time is not harder than the first. That reasoning is offered as a promise God has bound Himself to. The promise is called true, not likely. What follows is a split outcome, and the wording is careful. The reward is given with equity. The punishment is tied exactly to what people kept doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bodily resurrection was the point at which many listeners stopped, not the existence of God. Bones in the ground looked like the end of an argument, and the objection is quoted elsewhere in exactly those words. The surah answers it early and then leaves it, returning through story and sign rather than repeating the proof.

keyTerms.note: The verb for starting something with no model in front of you. Placing it beside the verb for repeating turns resurrection into the easier of the two acts, which is the whole force of the sentence.
Fairness as a settled share rather than as a feeling. Attached to reward, it rules out favouritism, and the classical readings note that God's generosity operates above the measure, never below it.
Water heated to its limit. The same root gives words for a close relative and for a fever, so the term carries nearness and heat together, which is why the image is drinking rather than burning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the measure of everything in that landscape. A caravan planned its stages by wells. A household showed its standing by what it could offer a guest to drink. Cool water was the first courtesy at any door. Boiling water set before a guest turns the deepest Arabian welcome inside out. That is why the image needed no explaining to its first hearers.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of starting creation with repeating it recurs across the Quran as a compact argument. This surah uses it twice within thirty-one ayat. The second time it becomes a challenge to name any partner who can do the same. Both places keep the two verbs side by side, so the second act is always heard as an echo of the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is presented as a matter of consistency, not of power alone. If the return is real, the moral weight of a life does not vanish with the body. Justice is then not limited to what courts can reach. The passage also binds God by His own promise. That is a striking move. The certainty offered rests on God being truthful. It does not rest on what the reader can imagine.

crossReferences.why: States the same argument as a principle, that repeating creation is easier for God than beginning it.
Answers the objection about decayed bones with the one who gave them life the first time.
Turns this pair of verbs into a direct question about whether any partner can do the same.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you rebuilt once: a friendship, a routine, a room after a move. Recall how the second attempt went compared with the first. You already know from small things that starting over is not the same as starting cold. Let that be what you carry into the next hard beginning you face this week.
studies.explainEasier: Everyone goes back to God in the end. He made everything the first time, and He will make it again. Then He will pay back fairly: good for those who believed, and pain for those who refused.

studies.title: Stations For The Moon
studies.meaning: Two lights are named with two different words, and the difference is deliberate. One blazes. The other is a milder light. Then the moon is given measured stations, and a purpose is attached to the measuring. People can count years and keep accounts. The passage treats the sky as an instrument as much as an ornament. It closes by saying none of this was made idly. The signs are set out in detail for those who will actually learn.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabia lived by a lunar calendar, and the sacred months that made pilgrimage and trade possible were fixed by the moon's cycle. Sky-watching was ordinary competence, not specialist knowledge. The surah is arguing that the same regularity everyone relied on for business is itself an argument, and that people who read the sky for profit might read it for meaning.

keyTerms.note: Light that a thing gives off from itself, with heat implied. The classical scholars noticed that the sun receives this word while the moon receives a gentler one, and treated the pairing as intentional.
The general word for light that lets things be seen. Al-Tabari and others read the contrast with the sun's word as marking a difference in kind, not merely in brightness.
The word for the halting places a traveller stops at on a route. Applied to the moon it turns the month into a journey with named stages, which is how Arabian navigators used it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan leaving Mecca timed its departure by the moon. It steered at night by stars whose rising points men had learned as children. Debts fell due at the new crescent. The truce months that let rival tribes trade at the fairs began and ended by the same sighting. Nobody in that audience needed this ayah explained. They needed the ordinary sky pointed at.
studies.didYouKnow: The stations of the moon were a working system in Arabia before Islam. There were twenty-eight recognised positions, used to track the year and predict rain. The word this ayah uses is the same one those watchers used. Elsewhere the Quran calls the crescents timetables for people. Again the sky is defined by what it lets people organise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Order in creation is given a purpose that includes the human being. The heavens are not simply large and impressive; they are calibrated, and the calibration is described as being for you. That joins two claims that often drift apart: that the universe is made with truth, and that it is made habitable. Knowledge, in this framing, is not opposed to wonder but is the form wonder takes.

crossReferences.why: Gives night and day the same double purpose, seeking provision and knowing the count of years.
Answers a question about the moon's phases by calling them timetables for people and pilgrimage.
Pairs the breaking of dawn with sun and moon set for calculation, ending on the same two names.

studies.applyIt: Find the moon tonight and note which shape it is. Then check it again in three days. Doing this twice is enough to feel the difference between knowing the moon has phases and watching one. The ayah connects counting to attention; most of us have the counting outsourced and have lost the watching.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sun bright and the moon a softer light. He set stages for the moon so people could count the years and keep track of time. None of it was made for nothing.

studies.title: Signs For The Watchful
studies.meaning: One short sentence gathers everything. The turning of night into day, and whatever God has made anywhere in the heavens and the earth. Both are called signs. The clause at the end is the interesting part. The signs are said to be there for people who keep a certain wariness before God, not for people who are clever. Early scholars read this to mean that the evidence is public. What lets a person be moved by it is a moral state, not a sharp mind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah closes a short sequence that began with creation and the Throne and moved through sun and moon. The surah is building an argument from what its audience already granted, before turning to what they denied. No specific occasion is reported for it; the setting is the general one of a city that acknowledged a creator and drew none of the conclusions.

keyTerms.note: The noun covers both difference and taking turns, from a root meaning to come after. Applied to night and day it names the handover itself, not the two states, which is where the regularity shows.
The same word used for verses of scripture. Using it for the sky puts creation and revelation in one category, two texts pointing the same direction, and the Quran keeps the overlap deliberately.
From a root meaning to take a shield. It describes a wariness that keeps a person from crossing certain lines, and the ayah makes that posture the condition for seeing what is plainly there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a desert climate the changeover between night and day is not slow. Heat drops fast after sunset, and the stars arrive quickly. Travel was arranged around that. The hardest stages were walked in darkness, and rest was taken through the worst of the sun. So the turn this ayah points at was a daily matter for its first hearers. Their bodies tracked it without instruments.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses one word both for a verse of scripture and for a feature of the natural world. This ayah applies it to the sky. Closing such a passage with a clause naming who benefits runs through this whole opening section. Each clause names a different group: people who know, people who are watchful, people who reflect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence is not treated here as neutral. The same sunrise stands in front of everyone, and the passage says only some read it, which locates the difference inside the observer. That resists two errors at once: the claim that proof compels belief, and the claim that faith has nothing to do with what can be seen. Attention is presented as the moral act, and the signs remain available for anyone who takes it up.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about night and day, naming people of understanding as the ones who see.
Expands the same list across winds, rain, ships and animals, all called signs for those who reason.
Runs the same catalogue three times, each time closing with a different qualifying clause.

studies.applyIt: Watch one sunset this week from beginning to end without a screen in your hand. It takes about twenty minutes. Do not try to feel anything in particular. The ayah does not ask for emotion, it asks for the kind of attention that most of us have quietly stopped paying to things that happen every single day.
studies.explainEasier: Night turns into day, and day turns into night. Look at everything God made in the sky and on the earth. All of it points to Him, for people who pay attention.

studies.title: Content And At Ease
studies.meaning: No argument is denied here and no doctrine is stated. What is described is a settling: not expecting to meet God, being satisfied with this life, and growing comfortable inside it. Alongside that runs an inattention to the signs. Early scholars note that the wording targets a way of living rather than a stated position, so a person could hold the right beliefs and still answer this description. The outcome named uses the word for shelter, which turns the sentence bitter.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience with a great deal to lose. The city's leading families were prosperous, their trade routes were secure, and the arrangement suited them. A message that made this life provisional threatened the settlement itself. The passage follows immediately on three ayat about signs in the sky and earth, so the heedlessness it names is heedlessness of something just placed in front of the reader.

keyTerms.note: From a root for level ground and a calmed heart. The word is usually warm in the Quran; used here of the present life it names a peace that has attached itself to the wrong thing.
Not ignorance but inattention. The root describes leaving something unattended rather than never having known it, so the charge is about where the eyes rest, not about missing information.
The place a traveller turns aside to for shelter, the same word used for the shade a herd gathers in. Applying it to the Fire makes what was sought as safety into the destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no farmland and no river. Its wealth came entirely from running a shrine and a trade route. So its prosperity felt like something people had built themselves. A merchant with two caravan seasons behind him, and a house near the sanctuary, had every reason to call his position settled. That satisfaction is the thing this passage names. Not poverty, and not luxury.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for growing settled and at rest appears elsewhere in the Quran for hearts that find rest in the remembrance of God. It appears again for a soul addressed as calm at the point of return. The same root that names the deepest peace a person can have is used here for the shallowest. Only the thing it attaches to changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts unbelief in the direction of a life, not in a stated claim. What is criticised is not enjoying the world. It is taking the world as final, treating what you can see as the whole account. That leaves ordinary comfort alone. It asks instead what a person rests their weight on. It also implies that expectation shapes conduct. What you take to be coming decides what you find worth doing now.

crossReferences.why: States the same preference plainly, that people choose the present life though the next is better and lasting.
Uses the same verb for hearts growing settled, but attached to the remembrance of God instead.
Draws the contrast in terms of provision, what you are given now against what God keeps.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would be most reluctant to lose, and be honest rather than pious about the answer. Then notice how much of this week was arranged around protecting it. The passage is not asking you to give it up. It is asking whether you have quietly begun treating it as the point of the whole thing.
studies.explainEasier: Some people do not expect to meet God. They are happy with this life and settle down in it, and they pay no attention to His signs. The Fire will be their home.

studies.title: Guided By Their Faith
studies.meaning: The short phrase in the middle carries the weight: their Lord guides them by their faith. Early scholars divide over what it points to. Some read it as guidance in this life given in proportion to belief already held, so that acting on what you know earns more to act on. Others read it as light on the Day of return, faith itself becoming the thing that shows the way forward. Both readings agree that guidance is not a single event but something that accumulates.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, set directly against the description before it. The surah has just named people who settled into this life and stopped noticing. This ayah names the opposite case in the same grammatical shape, and it begins with the same words. The classical scholars read the two as a pair. Neither sentence explains itself alone.

keyTerms.note: From a root for showing the road and for a gift. The verb is continuous, which is why the early scholars read it as ongoing direction rather than an initial rescue from error.
The attached particle can mean because of or by means of, and the tradition preserves both. Faith is either the reason guidance is given or the instrument through which it is walked.
From a root meaning softness and comfort, the opposite of hardship rather than of poverty. It names the quality of the gardens, not their contents, so the phrase describes a condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guides were hired, not borrowed. A merchant crossing to Syria paid a man who knew where the wells sat and which route was open that season. Following him closely was the difference between arriving and not. Everyone knew that a guide is only useful to someone already walking. The picture of rivers running underneath was just as solid to people whose water came up from wells by rope.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of six places where the Quran names the Gardens of Bliss. It is the only one that ties entry to being guided by faith rather than to deeds alone. Across the Quran, rivers running beneath is the most common single image of the garden. It is repeated far more often than any description of what grows there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as responsive. It comes to those who already believe. That makes belief a beginning, not a finish line. It also rules out treating direction from God as a one-time delivery. The passage links inner state to final destination, but not mechanically. What is promised is a place. The road to it runs through what the person already holds and keeps acting on.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing in different words: those who are guided, He increases in guidance.
Attaches guidance of the heart to belief in a moment of disaster, the practical form of this promise.
Shows faith becoming visible light running ahead of believers on the Day of return.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you already know is right and have not been doing, and do it once today. Small is better. The ayah describes guidance arriving through faith rather than before it, and the ordinary experience matches: clarity about the next step usually shows up after you take the one you were avoiding.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good get help from their Lord because of their faith. He guides them along. In the end they get gardens of happiness with rivers flowing under them.

studies.title: The Last Of Their Call
studies.meaning: The whole speech of the garden is given in one line, and it has three parts. It opens by declaring God free of every defect, it passes sideways into a greeting exchanged between people, and it closes on praise. What is missing is asking. The word used for their call normally introduces a request, and here it contains none, which the early scholars read as the sign that nothing is left wanting. Worship continues after need has ended.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a short passage that has just set two ways of living side by side. The surah is describing outcomes, not reporting an occasion. Its first hearers knew what a life of asking sounded like. Prayer at the sanctuary was largely a matter of asking for rain, safe passage and children. The picture drawn here removes exactly that element.

keyTerms.note: From the root for summoning and for supplication, the same one behind the ordinary word for prayer of request. Its use for speech containing no request is what gives the ayah its point.

A declaration that God is far removed from any deficiency, built on a root suggesting swimming or moving freely away. It clears ground rather than describing, denying limits before anything is affirmed.
From a root meaning life, so a greeting is literally a wish that the other live. That the greeting exchanged is peace makes the social air of the place part of its description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greeting was serious business in a tribal society. The words two parties exchanged when they met on a road announced whether this was a meeting or a threat. Travellers rehearsed them. A wrong greeting could start something. Peace as the standing word in the garden would have landed first as the removal of all that reckoning. A whole kind of watchfulness switched off.
studies.didYouKnow: The final words placed in the mouths of the people of the garden are the same words that open the Quran's first surah, praise to God, Lord of the Worlds. The classical scholars noticed the loop: the Book begins where the destination ends. The greeting named in the middle also becomes the greeting of the community in this life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is shown to outlast its usual motives. Praise continues where there is no danger, no shortage and nothing to ask for. So it was never only a trade. The reward turns out to include the very thing that was asked of people. The order matters too. God is glorified first. Peace passes between people second. Gratitude comes last, as a response rather than a prompt.

crossReferences.why: The Quran opens with the exact words this ayah gives as the last speech of the garden.
Names the same greeting of peace as what those admitted to the gardens say to each other.
Shows praise arriving as the first response once sorrow has been lifted away entirely.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your talking to God this week was a request. Not to criticise it, since asking is invited elsewhere in the Book. Just add one sentence at the end of a prayer that asks for nothing at all. Say it after the request, in the order this ayah uses, and see whether it changes the shape of the whole.
studies.explainEasier: In the garden, people say how perfect God is. They greet each other with peace. And the last thing they say is praise to God, the Lord of all the worlds.

studies.title: If Harm Came As Fast
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence measures one thing against another. People press for good to arrive quickly; suppose harm were delivered at that same speed. The classical scholars take this in two ways, either of the curses people utter in anger, or of the punishment sceptics dared God to send. Under either reading the answer is the same: their appointed span would already be over. What follows is not comfort. Being left to wander in one's own excess is described as a consequence, not a reprieve.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some in the city had openly challenged God to rain stones on them if the message were true, a demand the Quran records elsewhere in their own words. The passage answers a taunt without answering it on its terms. Every delay they read as proof of nothing happening is presented instead as a term still running.

keyTerms.note: The root carries both speed and impatience, and the Quran uses it elsewhere to say the human being was made of haste. Here the same verb is applied first to God, then to people.
A fixed period with a known end, the word used for the due date of a debt. It names a length of time rather than a moment, so what is finished is a span, not an event.
From a root describing water that rises past its banks. It pictures wrongdoing as overflow rather than as trespass, something that spreads by its own pressure once nothing checks it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cursing was ordinary speech. A man who lost a camel, or quarrelled with a cousin, would call ruin down on him in front of witnesses. Poets built reputations on long, elaborate curses against rival tribes. Nobody expected any of it to be enforced. A world where every angry sentence took effect at once would have emptied the peninsula within a season. The first hearers knew that.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah belongs to a small group that argue the same way, by supposing God acted at once. Two of them say that if He seized people for what they had earned, not one living creature would be left on the earth. In each case the sentence is built as a condition contrary to fact. So the delay is how things actually are. It is not a favour granted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Holding back is shown as a choice, not an absence. That makes ordinary time itself a gift rather than a neutral background. The passage also refuses to read unanswered defiance as evidence either way. Most seriously, it describes being left alone as worse than being stopped. When nothing interrupts a person, the wandering goes on. Having no check turns out to be its own kind of verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the human tendency exactly, praying for evil as one prays for good, out of haste.
Makes the same unreal condition explicit, that immediate reckoning would leave nothing alive.
Records the taunt this ayah answers, a demand that stones be rained down from the sky.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for in anger and did not get. A confrontation you wanted, a message you nearly sent, a wish about someone who had wronged you. Most people have at least one they are now relieved about. Let that be the concrete form of this ayah rather than an idea, and notice what the delay did for you.
studies.explainEasier: People want good things to come fast. If God sent harm that fast, their time would already be over. Instead He leaves some people alone to keep going too far.

studies.title: Lying, Sitting, Standing
studies.meaning: Three postures are listed in a rising order. Early scholars read them as covering every condition a person can pray from, starting with the one who cannot get up. That is how thoroughly trouble produces prayer. Then relief arrives and the man walks on. The comparison is exact: as if he had never called at all. The closing clause widens the case. This is how conduct comes to look fine to people who go past limits.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience whose religion was largely transactional. Petitions were made at the sanctuary in emergencies and vows were paid when the emergency passed. The passage does not report a particular incident. It describes a pattern the surah will return to twice more, once at sea in a storm and once after relief from hardship, each time with the same shape and different scenery.

keyTerms.note: Damage that reaches a person's body or livelihood, distinguished from harm someone does to another. The word appears twice in this ayah, once as what arrives and once as what is lifted.
A plain verb of movement, not of denial or rebellion. The choice is deliberate: nothing dramatic happens, the man simply continues on his way, which is what makes the picture recognisable.
From a root for exceeding a proper measure, used of spending and of conduct alike. It names people who have lost a sense of proportion rather than people committing one identifiable offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Illness in that world was largely waited out. There were bonesetters, the burning of a wound to close it, and cures of honey and herbs. But for a fever the household could do little but keep the sick person cool and watch. Long hours flat on a mat, with nothing to do but ask, were the ordinary way of being unwell. The ayah starts from exactly that position and works upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three postures appear elsewhere in the Quran in the reverse order: standing, sitting and lying on their sides. There they describe people who remember God in every condition. Read together, the two lists use one set of body positions to mark opposite habits. One group prays through all of them only under pressure. The other prays through all of them anyway.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats forgetting, not denying, as the typical human failure. Nothing is argued and nothing is given up. A man simply resumes. That is a harder thing to hear than rebellion, because it takes no decision at all. It also implies that a crisis shows something true about a person. The prayer offered flat on his back was not false. It was simply held up by nothing once the pressure lifted.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical sequence with the added detail that he forgets what he had been praying for.
Reverses the order to show the same man withdrawing in comfort and praying at length in trouble.
Uses the same three postures for those who remember God continuously, not only under pressure.

studies.applyIt: Remember something you badly wanted and eventually received. Go back and find what you promised while you were waiting. Then check honestly whether you kept it. If you did not, pick one small piece of that promise and do it this week, without telling anyone. That is the ayah's whole subject, handled at the scale you can actually reach.
studies.explainEasier: When trouble hits, a person calls on God lying down, sitting, or standing. But once the trouble is gone, he walks away as if he never called at all.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: To See How You Behave
studies.meaning: Two sentences run a whole history in miniature. Earlier peoples were removed once their wrongdoing was clear and the evidence had reached them. The order is stated carefully: the messengers came first. Then the address turns to the listeners. They are told they stand on ground the earlier ones left. Early scholars read the clause about seeing how you behave as bringing into the open what God already knows. The record is made, not discovered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Trade caravans from Mecca passed abandoned settlements on both the northern and southern routes, and the Quran elsewhere tells its audience that they walk by such places morning and evening. The argument works because the ruins were part of ordinary geography. Nothing in the passage points to one occasion; it appeals to a landscape the merchants of the city crossed every season.

keyTerms.note: The word means both a generation of people and the span they occupy. Scholars differ on the length intended, giving figures from forty years upward, and none of the classical readings insists on a number.
Plural of the word for one who comes after and takes another's place. It carries no honour by itself, only the fact of standing where someone else stood and inheriting the same conditions.
A verb of looking, not of finding out. The early scholars explain it as knowledge becoming visible in events, so that conduct is produced and witnessed rather than predicted from the outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The peninsula was full of the leftovers of people who had done better than the current occupants. Carved facades stood in the rock north of Medina, dams and irrigation channels lay broken in the south, and place names preserved tribes that no longer existed. A merchant could water his camels at a well dug by a vanished people. Succession was not an abstraction; it was where you camped.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about being made successors, so that God may see how you behave, appears in almost the same words in another surah. There Moses says it to Israelites who were being persecuted and were promised the land of those who oppressed them. In both places the promise of inheritance arrives with the same condition attached. That turns a reward into a job.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Inheritance is presented as a test, not a verdict. Holding a place proves nothing about deserving it. The people before also held it, and they were removed. So success is not an endorsement. Every generation stands where the last one stood. The mention of messengers arriving first also shows that no removal is described before the case was made.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same wording, promising succession in the land and then watching how people act.
Names the same role of successors and states directly that the differences between people are a test.
Points to earlier generations whose dwellings the audience physically walks through, as signs.

studies.applyIt: Find out who lived in your home before you did. A neighbour will often know, or the deeds will. Hold that for a moment: someone measured these rooms, argued in them, and left. You are the current occupant of a place that has had others and will have more. That is the ayah's exact posture, at the smallest scale available.
studies.explainEasier: God ended nations before you when they did wrong. Their messengers had come to them with clear signs, but they still would not believe. Now you live where they lived, so God can see what you will do.

studies.title: Bring Another Or Change It
studies.meaning: The request comes in two versions: a different recitation altogether, or an edited one. Early scholars note that what the objectors wanted cut were the passages against their images. The reply refuses on grounds of position, not preference. The one reciting has no right to revise what he did not compose. Then the answer turns personal. He says he is afraid of a great Day if he disobeys. That is an odd thing for a man inventing a religion to say about himself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Negotiation was the city's normal instrument, and the leadership had already tried offers of wealth and status. This is the same approach applied to the text: keep the message but drop the clauses that cost us. Reports of such approaches are widely transmitted in the classical sources, though they are attached to the period generally rather than to a single meeting.

keyTerms.note: The verb for swapping one thing for another, not for correcting an error. What was asked was a replacement of particular passages, which is why the answer speaks about authority rather than about accuracy.
Literally from the direction of myself. The phrase locates the source of speech, and by denying that source it separates the man from the words in the plainest terms available.
A passive form of a verb for swift, hidden communication. Keeping it passive leaves the speaker as recipient throughout the sentence, with no grammatical room to be the author.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the great art of Arabia, and poets revised all the time. A famous ode might be reworked over a season before the fair at Ukaz. Audiences knew a line could be improved, sold, or shaped to fit a patron who was paying. Against that background the request was entirely reasonable. It assumed the ordinary link between a maker and his material.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the objectors use for changing the text appears again in this same surah, forty-nine ayat later. There it stands in the statement that there is no altering the words of God. The demand and its answer are built on one root. So the surah refuses the request twice. Once in the reply given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and once as a plain fact about the words themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is defined by what the receiver cannot do with it. A messenger who could adjust the message would be its author. The whole category would collapse into authorship. The passage also makes fear part of the evidence. The person best placed to know whether the words were his own is the one most afraid of touching them. Obedience here is shown as a limit, not a privilege.

crossReferences.why: States the consequence in the strongest terms if the messenger had attributed any words to God himself.
Answers the demand later in this surah, saying there is no alteration to the words of God.
Describes the pressure to invent something else against God, and how close it came to working.

studies.applyIt: Think of a text you are bound by and cannot edit. A contract, a diagnosis, a message from someone who has died. Notice how differently you read something you are not allowed to adjust. Then read a page of the Quran today in that same posture. Resist the small private edits we all make to soften what we would rather it said.
studies.explainEasier: Some people asked for a different Quran, or for this one to be changed. The answer was that he could not change it himself. He only follows what God sends him.

studies.title: A Lifetime Before It
studies.meaning: The answer to the demand for an edited recitation moves in two steps. First, none of this was at the reciter's disposal: had God willed otherwise, they would never have heard it and would not even have known of it. Second, an appeal to a life already on record among the same listeners, with nothing of this kind in it. Then the charge is turned around. Fabricating about God describes the people asserting divine partners, not the man refusing to revise what he was given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources place the beginning of revelation around the Prophet's fortieth year, so the span he points to was not a claim requiring proof. It was the shared memory of the audience. Everyone hearing the argument had known him as a young man, and several had employed him or done business with him. The argument works only in a small city, which is where it was made.

keyTerms.note: The word for the whole length of a life, left indefinite here so it reads as a considerable stretch. What is being offered as evidence is duration, the sheer number of years available for inspection.
From a root for cutting and shaping leather. The image is manufacture rather than error, something worked into a convincing form, which is why it carries no excuse of honest mistake.
The root belongs to the farmer who splits open the ground. Success in this word means breaking through to something buried, so the denial is that fabrication ever reaches anything real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that a man's history belonged to everyone. Family lines were memorised. Quarrels were remembered across generations. Poets kept the record of who had behaved well and who had not. A merchant hiring a caravan agent asked around rather than reading references. In a place built entirely out of reputation, forty quiet years were an argument that needed no witnesses called.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran makes this argument from absence in more than one form. Elsewhere it points out that the man delivering the message had read no scripture before. It says he had written none with his right hand. Another place says he had known neither what the Book was nor what faith was. Each version rests on what was missing from a life, not on what was in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is treated as something a whole life either supports or does not. Against a charge of invention, the reply is not a miracle but a life. So part of a message's credibility sits in the character of the one carrying it. The reversal that follows is just as pointed. The real invention is what people say about God. That offence is set higher here than any other.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same argument from what was absent before, no scripture read and nothing written.
Repeats the question about who does greater wrong, and shows the witnesses testifying on that Day.
Says he knew neither Book nor faith beforehand, which is the positive form of this argument.

studies.applyIt: Consider what someone who has known you for ten years could say about your consistency. Not your best moments, your ordinary ones. Then pick a single small thing you say you believe and check whether the past month supports it. A life is the slowest argument available and the only one nobody can rehearse.
studies.explainEasier: If God had not wanted it, you would never have heard this Quran at all. I lived among you for years before it came. No one does more wrong than a person who makes up lies about God.

studies.title: Informing God Of Something
studies.meaning: Two observations take a practice apart. The objects served can do neither harm nor good. That removes any working reason to serve them. The defence offered was that they carry requests upward. The reply is a question sharp enough to be missed on a first reading. If such an arrangement existed, God would know about it. To claim it is to tell God a fact about His own heavens and earth that had escaped Him. Early scholars treat this one question as the whole argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sanctuary at the centre of the city held images that were not understood as rivals to a supreme God. They were understood as brokers, and the Quran elsewhere quotes the exact defence in the objectors' own words. This is why the surah keeps returning to intercession rather than to the existence of God, which almost nobody in that audience denied.

keyTerms.note: Plural of the one who joins his plea to another's, with a possessive ending attached. The claimed relationship is personal and proprietary, and it is precisely that ownership the question examines.
The verb for delivering news of consequence, sharing a root with the word for tidings a prophet brings. Turned back on the objectors, it casts them as the ones announcing something to God.
From a root for height, in a form suggesting distance already established rather than elevation achieved. It closes the ayah by placing God out of range of the arrangement just described.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Go-betweens were how business got done. A trader arriving from Yemen found a Meccan to stand for him. A debtor found a man of standing to speak to his creditor. Protection for a stranger was arranged through whoever had the ear of the right family. The fee for such introductions was ordinary and openly paid. Worship took over the same structure. This ayah takes that structure apart, not the sincerity of the people using it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere quotes the defence this ayah answers almost word for word: we serve them only to bring us nearer to God. The same passages describe those supposed helpers disowning the arrangement entirely on the Day of Resurrection. Across the Quran, speaking up for someone before God is never denied outright. Every passage on it turns instead on whose permission it needs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge, not power, is the hinge of the argument. If God knows everything in the heavens and earth, then an unknown office cannot exist. So the whole system of brokered access collapses, with no word said about the idols themselves. That leaves the reader with one sharp point. Much of what people aim at God is really aimed at their own picture of how access works. The passage asks where that picture came from.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same defence, that these are served only to bring the worshipper nearer to God.
Shows the outcome, when no intercessors are found among the idols and partners are disowned.
States that those called on cannot hear, and would not answer even if they could.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing this week that you treat as a channel to God rather than as a good in itself: a person, a place, a routine, a phrase you repeat. There is nothing wrong with any of them. Just check whether you have started to feel that without it your request would not get through.
studies.explainEasier: Some people worship things that cannot hurt them or help them. They say these things speak for them with God. But God knows everything in the sky and on the earth already.

studies.title: Mankind Was One Community
studies.meaning: Unity comes first and division second. Early scholars differ over which period the single community belonged to. Some point to the generations between Adam and Noah. Others point to the household that survived the flood. The sources record the range without settling it. What follows explains why the argument is still running. A decision God already took holds judgement back. So disputes that could be closed at once are left open. The delay is not indifference. It is a stated policy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah dealing with the objectors' demands. The audience lived among many competing cults. They knew religious difference as an ordinary fact of the trade routes. What the ayah supplies is a history for that fact. Related passages elsewhere describe division arriving after knowledge came, out of rivalry among those who had received it.

keyTerms.note: The first word covers any group bound by something shared, from a nation to a way of life. Paired with one, it describes agreement rather than mere numbers living side by side.

From a root for coming after and taking turns, so difference is pictured as people falling out of step. The prefixed particle makes it consequence rather than accident, following directly from what preceded.
A decision already issued, using a verb of racing ahead. It names a ruling made in advance that now governs the present, which is why the case cannot simply be closed now.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage season brought tribes with different gods into one valley under a truce. Their differences were managed, not resolved. Disputes over water, grazing and blood debts were settled by arbitration. Everyone knew that some quarrels were left standing on purpose. Closing them would cost more than living with them. The ayah borrows that familiar logic and applies it upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this history twice in nearly the same words. The second version adds what happened in between. God sent prophets and scripture to judge between people. The disagreement broke out afterwards, among those who had received the Book. Another passage names the cause plainly as rivalry, not confusion. That changes what kind of problem division is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Religious disagreement is given a beginning. So it is not the permanent condition of the human race. It also means the current state of the argument is not the verdict. The delay is tied to a decree made earlier. That removes any warrant for forcing an outcome now. It also puts the settling of disputes at a point none of the parties controls. Judgement is put off, not cancelled.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller version, prophets and scripture sent, and division breaking out after the proofs came.
Uses the same phrase about a prior decree and names resentment as the cause of division.
States that God could have made one community and did not, and connects that to mercy.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind a disagreement in your family or community that nobody can win. Consider that it may be one of the things left open rather than a failure of yours to close it. Then decide how you will behave inside it this month, which is the part actually assigned to you.
studies.explainEasier: People were all one group at first. Then they began to disagree. God had already chosen to wait before judging them. So their arguments were left open, not settled right away.

studies.title: So Wait, I Am Waiting
studies.meaning: A demand for a sign is met with a statement about who decides, not with a refusal. What is hidden belongs to God. That puts the timing and the choice of any sign outside the messenger's authority, and outside the questioners' bargaining. Then comes the unexpected part. He is told to say wait, and at once to add that he is waiting with them. Early scholars read this as putting both sides in the same position before an outcome neither can force. That is a strange thing to concede under pressure to perform.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands for a great sign are recorded again and again in this period. Sometimes the demand named what the sign should be: a spring made to gush, a garden, a treasure, an angel seen beside the messenger. The Quran answers such requests in several places without granting them. Each time it points back to signs already there, rather than promising new ones.

keyTerms.note: From a root for something absent or sunk out of view, like a sun below the horizon. It names what is real but withheld, not what is unknowable in principle, and the Quran keeps it as God's own domain.
The same word used for a verse of scripture and for a feature of the natural world. The objectors are asking for one kind while standing inside another, which is the quiet irony of the request.
From a root for looking out for something expected. Placing the messenger inside this group makes waiting a shared condition rather than a punishment assigned to the other side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting was a skill in that economy. A family with capital in a caravan waited months for news, and there was no way to hurry it or to learn anything before the riders appeared on the northern track. Rain was waited for in the same way, watched for in cloud shapes and never commanded. The ayah asks for a posture its first hearers practised every year.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records requests for a sign several times. It never has the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) produce one on demand. Each time the reply hands the matter back to God. One place adds that God is able to send a sign, but most people do not know. The refusal is steady enough across the text to count as a position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The limits of a prophet are drawn here as sharply as his authority is drawn elsewhere. He holds the message, not the evidence. That keeps revelation from becoming a performance judged on its effects. Putting the unseen entirely with God also undoes the assumption behind the demand, that faith should arrive as force. And the shared waiting makes a quiet claim. Whatever is coming will be plain to both sides.

crossReferences.why: Answers the identical demand by saying God is able to send a sign, though most do not know.
Meets the same request with the messenger's job description, a warner, with a guide for every people.
States plainly that signs are with God alone, and the messenger is only a clear warner.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are currently waiting on that no amount of effort will speed up. A result, a decision from someone else, a body healing. Notice how much energy goes into trying to hurry it. Try setting that energy down for a single day and see what it was costing you.
studies.explainEasier: Some people wanted a miracle sent down to prove it. The answer was that only God knows what is hidden. So wait, and I will wait with you.

studies.title: Swifter In Planning
studies.meaning: Relief arrives, and the first use made of it is to work against the signs. The word for that scheming is then applied to God. The classical scholars are careful here. Used of people it means a plan kept from its target. Used of God it means the answering move that meets such a plan, with nothing hidden or false in it. The closing line lowers the heat. It simply notes that the schemes are being written down as they are made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has already described a man praying through illness and walking away once it lifts. This ayah repeats the movement at the level of a whole people and adds what they do with the recovered time. No single occasion is reported; drought, sickness and failed caravans were recurrent enough in that region for the pattern to be observed rather than dated.

keyTerms.note: The verb for a first small sample of something rather than a full portion. Applied to mercy, it frames relief as a sip offered, which quietly measures how little was needed to change the behaviour.
A plan kept from the one it targets. The early scholars note that when the word is used of God it means His countering measure and carries no deception, since nothing about His response is concealed.
Here understood by the early scholars as the recording angels rather than human messengers. The same word covers both, which puts the quiet clerical work beside the public preaching.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Written records were rare and valuable in Mecca. Debts, treaties and the terms of a partnership were mostly held in memory and confirmed by witnesses. A document was drawn up only when the sum was large. So to say that something is being written down was to say it is serious business. The image is a ledger opened for dealings nobody thought were being logged.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes recording angels in several places. One passage calls them honourable scribes who know everything people do. Another says they are close by, writing down secrets and private talks. This ayah adds a detail those passages leave out. What gets recorded includes the planning stage, before anything has been carried out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ingratitude is shown as active, not passive. The people in this ayah do not merely forget relief. They use it. That makes thanklessness a form of work. It also explains why the Quran treats gratitude as a discipline rather than a mood. The answering move is called swifter. So safety does not lie in out-planning God. It lies in dropping the plan altogether.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same alternation from the other side, rejoicing in mercy and despairing when harm comes.
Shows a concrete plot met by God's planning, with the same contrast of the two words.
Describes the honourable recorders watching over people and knowing everything they do.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time something you dreaded resolved itself. Recall the first three days afterwards and what you did with them. Most of us spend recovered time immediately, without marking it. Take twenty minutes this week and write down one relief you received this year, with the date. That is the smallest possible ledger of your own.
studies.explainEasier: When God gives people relief after trouble, some of them start plotting against His signs. God can move faster than any plot. And His angels write down everything they plan.

studies.title: A Favourable Wind Turns
studies.meaning: A voyage is narrated in miniature: good wind, pleasure taken in it, then a gale and waves closing from every direction. At the point where they conclude they are surrounded, something happens to their worship. It becomes exclusive, with nothing left in it for anyone but God, and a bargain is offered along with it. Early scholars note that this is presented as the natural state of a person stripped of options, which is why the passage does not praise the prayer. It examines what happens next.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who financed sea trade even if they rarely sailed. Meccan money moved goods through Red Sea ports toward Yemen and the north. The risks were understood in detail, because they were priced. Storms, piracy and total loss were part of the sums every season. That makes this the most business-minded image in the surah.

keyTerms.note: One of the words that stays the same whether one vessel is meant or many, its number shown only by the verbs around it. Here the verbs are plural, so a whole fleet is caught at once.
From a root for separating a thing from what is mixed with it, as cream is drawn off milk. Sincerity in this word is subtraction, the removal of every other party from the transaction.
A passive from the root for surrounding, used of a wall around a garden or an army around a town. It names the moment escape stops being imaginable, which is when the wording changes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian sailors feared the Red Sea for good reason. Coral shoals lay close to the surface, and the coast offered few safe landings. Ships hugged the shore and moved by daylight. A wind from the wrong quarter could put a vessel on the reef within an hour. Everyone in Mecca knew someone whose goods had gone down. Shares in a voyage were spread across several hulls to survive that.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for making religion purely God's own occurs seven times in the Quran. In three of them, including this one, it is spoken by people caught in a storm at sea. Classical scholars of style also cite this ayah as a standard case of a sudden change of person. The ayah begins by addressing you directly. Then it shifts mid-sentence to describing them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grants something uncomfortable. Pure belief in one God is available to almost anyone under enough pressure. Sincerity produced by terror is real while it lasts, and the Quran does not deny it. What it questions is whether an emergency is a discovery or only a pause. That leaves the reader with a sharper test than belief. The test is what the same person does with dry land.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same story in one sentence, sincere prayer at sea and partners ascribed on shore.
Adds the detail of waves like canopies, and notes that only some waver once delivered.
Says the ones they usually call on vanish at sea, leaving only Him, and names the turning away.

studies.applyIt: Recall the most frightened you have been and what you said in that moment. It was probably very short and very clear. Say that same thing once today, out loud, while nothing at all is wrong. You will find it harder than it was during the storm, and noticing that difficulty is the point.
studies.explainEasier: God carries people over land and sea. On a ship in a good wind they are happy. Then a storm hits and waves close in, and they call on God alone to save them.

studies.title: Against Your Own Souls
studies.meaning: Rescue is followed at once by aggression. The address switches from story to a direct call to all people. The central claim is that overreaching lands on the one who does it. Early scholars read this as more than a warning about consequences. The harm is not only repaid later. It is already being done to the doer, since a person who takes what is not theirs has changed what they are. What such action buys is then priced honestly, as the enjoyment of a passing life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Feuds in Arabia typically began as a claim pressed too far, and the retaliation cycles that followed could outlast the people who started them. A city that lived by protecting caravans understood the cost of aggression as an economic fact. The ayah follows a storm at sea and applies the same lesson on land, where the sense of being surrounded fades and the old habits return.

keyTerms.note: From a root for seeking, which slides into seeking beyond one's share. The word covers both wanting and taking, so the wrong begins in the appetite rather than at the moment of the act.
The same root turned into a noun and given back to the addressees. Repeating the word within two clauses ties the deed and its return together in a way the translation cannot quite hold.
Goods a traveller carries for the road, useful and temporary by definition. Calling the gain of aggression this word prices it exactly: real, usable, and not something you arrive with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood money existed because the other option was ruin. A killing could commit two clans to years of raids. Elders settled payment in camels exactly to stop a wrong from becoming an inheritance. Everyone had heard of feuds that ate up more men than the first dispute ever involved. That was the practical form of a wrong coming back on the people who started it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states the principle in several forms. One passage says evil scheming overwhelms none but its authors, another that blame lies on those who wrong people and commit aggression without right. Later in this same surah the point is made in its bluntest version: God does not wrong people in the least, but people wrong their own selves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Wrongdoing is described as self-directed before it is described as punishable. That does not deny the victim's injury. But it puts the deepest damage in the one who commits it, which changes what justice is for. The passage also refuses to call gains from injustice unreal. They are called enjoyment, plainly. Then they are placed inside a life that ends with a return and an account.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule directly, that evil scheming overwhelms nobody except the ones who author it.
Places blame precisely on those who wrong people and overreach in the land without right.
Gives the sharpest version later in this surah, that people wrong only themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of an argument where you were mostly right and pressed further than you needed to. Notice what that extra pressing did to you rather than to them. If the person is still reachable, say one sentence acknowledging the overreach. Not the substance of the dispute. Only the part where you took more ground than the case required.
studies.explainEasier: God saves people from the storm. Then they go straight back to doing wrong on the earth. The wrong they do really lands on them. It buys a little comfort now, and then they go back to God.

studies.title: As If It Never Flourished
studies.meaning: The comparison is built to arrive late. Water falls, plants mix with the soil, people and animals feed, and the field reaches the exact moment of its beauty. Only then does the sentence name what has been growing alongside the crop, which is the owners' conviction that they have the thing under control. The reversal comes by night or by day, unspecified, and what is left is stubble. The closing phrase makes reflection the whole purpose of telling it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Farming in the peninsula depended on rain that could fail entirely or arrive as a flood. The oasis settlements around Mecca lived with both. The Quran uses this image in several surahs. Here it comes straight after people are rescued from a storm and go back to overreaching. So the parable answers a question about confidence, not about farming.

keyTerms.note: The word means gilding and decoration, and gives its name to another surah. Applied to a field at its peak it suggests something applied to a surface rather than grown from within.
From the root for measuring and for power. The claim is not ownership but mastery, a settled sense that the outcome is now theirs to determine, which is the exact assumption the ayah tests.
What is left standing after a harvest, dry and worthless. The word occurs only twice in the Quran, and the other place uses it of a people who had been calling out until they were silenced.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in that landscape was watched with an intensity hard to convey. Wadis that had been dry for a season could run within an hour and be gone by evening, and a family's whole year turned on where a cloud released its load. Farmers at Taif and in the oases read cloud direction the way sailors read wind. Everyone had also seen a standing crop taken by hail, locusts or flood in a single night.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the earth's finery is the same word that names one of the Quran's surahs, and it is used elsewhere for ornamented speech that deceives. The word for what the field becomes appears only twice in the whole Quran. The second occurrence describes a people who kept crying out until they were made silent ash.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable targets one moment, not wealth itself. Nothing is criticised until the owners believe they have mastered what they were given. That is where the danger sits. The passage also refuses to make the timing knowable. It says by night or by day. So no one can arrange their confidence around a schedule. Reflection, not fear, is named as the response being asked for.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same parable compressed, water sent down, plants absorbing it, then debris scattered by wind.
Runs the identical image and names the things it stands for: play, glitter, boasting and rivalry.
Follows the water further, through underground wells to plants that yellow and turn to debris.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you have worked on for years and are quietly proud of. Ask what portion of it you actually arranged: the health, the timing, the people who happened to say yes. Do not talk yourself out of the pride. Just get the proportions right, which is the only thing the parable asks of anyone.
studies.explainEasier: This life is like rain that makes plants grow. The land looks lovely, and people think they own it. Then God's command comes at night or by day, and it is all cut down.

studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: Two motions are described and they are not the same. God calls to the Home of Peace, and He guides whom He wills to a straight path, so an open invitation and a particular guiding stand together in one sentence. Early scholars keep both without dissolving the tension. Then the reward: goodness, and something extra which is left unnamed. The explanation most often given for the addition is the sight of God, though the verse says only more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah largely taken up with people who wanted a different kind of sign and who treated this life as the whole account. The passage arrives just after a parable comparing worldly life to plants that flourish and are cut down overnight. Early scholars read the invitation as the answer to that parable. They record no specific occasion for the verses themselves.

keyTerms.note: The word for a dwelling with a courtyard, a household rather than a building. Joined to a word for wholeness and safety, it names the destination as a place to live in rather than a state to reach.
A plain word for addition, left without an object. Early scholars most often explain it as the sight of God, and note that the verse deliberately leaves the extra unspecified.
A film of dust or smoke settling on something, the darkening that comes over a face at bad news. Denying it is a physical description, since the face is where humiliation shows first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces were read constantly in that society. Think of a man returning from a failed deal, a family that had lost a claim, a debtor passing his creditor. Everyone knew the news before anybody spoke. Poetry describes the dust of shame settling on a man's features. Promising that neither dust nor lowness would touch these faces spoke to a culture where standing was worn openly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase Home of Peace only twice, here and at 6:127. In both places it is paired with a statement about God's relation to those who receive it. The word for peace inside it is the same one used as the greeting exchanged there. So the destination is named after what is said inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation is open to all and the guiding is particular. The passage sets them side by side without softening either. Classical discussion has kept both. It treats the call as genuinely addressed to everyone, while the arrival is not in human hands alone. The reward then refuses to be measured. Goodness is matched to what was done, and something further is added with no stated equivalent.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, adding that He is their ally.
Precedes it with the parable of vegetation cut down that this invitation answers.
States the principle of matching, that the reward of good is nothing but good.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the word peace passes your lips today as a greeting, and let one of those be deliberate. The destination in this verse is named after that word. It costs nothing to mean it once, and the passage suggests the greeting and the address are the same thing at different distances.
studies.explainEasier: God is calling people to the Home of Peace. Those who do good will get good back, and more besides. No dust or shame will settle on their faces. They will live in the Garden for ever.

studies.title: No Shield Against God
studies.meaning: Recompense is stated with unusual precision. What is returned for a bad deed is its like, matched rather than multiplied, and the early scholars contrast this with the generosity described for good deeds a verse earlier. Then two things are added that are not measured. Humiliation covers them, and no protector stands between them and God. The final image is faces wrapped in pieces of night, which answers the faces in the preceding ayah that carry neither gloom nor shame.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah is the second half of a pair, and reading it apart from its partner loses the structure. The preceding lines describe the home of peace and those who did well; this one supplies the matching case clause by clause. The surah is setting out outcomes at this stage rather than reporting an event, and no specific occasion is recorded for either half.

keyTerms.note: An exact equivalent, no more. The word draws a boundary around punishment that the neighbouring description of reward does not have, since that one adds an unspecified increase on top.
From a root meaning to hold something back from harm, used of a rope, a stronghold or a patron. It occurs three times in the Quran, each time in a scene where no such protection is found.
Sections cut from something larger, here from the night itself. The plural matters: not one covering but many separate patches laid over the face, which is what makes the image so strange.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a named relationship. A man travelled under the guarantee of a clan. To lose it was to become fair game on any road. Withdrawal of protection was announced in public, because its whole value lay in everyone knowing. To say a person has no protector at all was the fullest description of exposure that world had. It needed nothing added.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah mirrors the one before it phrase by phrase. That one promises goodness and more, and denies that gloom or shame will reach their faces; this one gives an exact equivalent, brings shame over them, and covers their faces in darkness. The Quran often builds such pairs, but few match so closely that each clause has a partner.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice and generosity work on different scales here. Wrong is answered in kind. That sets a ceiling on payback and rules out excess. The reward described beside it deliberately goes past its measure. That gap is a claim about God, not about what people deserve. The denial of any protector then removes the last assumption the passage has been taking apart. Access and shelter cannot be arranged through someone else.

crossReferences.why: The matching half of the pair, promising goodness and more, with no gloom reaching their faces.
Uses the same contrast of faces on that Day, some brightened and some darkened.
Sets radiant, laughing faces beside faces covered with misery and overwhelmed by darkness.

studies.applyIt: Notice the arrangements you keep in place in case things go wrong: the contact who could fix it, the savings, the person who would speak for you. None of them is a fault. Just spend a minute today acknowledging that each of them is itself something given to you, and that the list has an end.
studies.explainEasier: People who earn bad deeds get back exactly what they did. Shame will cover them. No one will keep them safe from God. Their faces will look dark, like bits of night.

studies.title: It Was Not Us You Served
studies.meaning: A scene is staged rather than described. Everyone is gathered, the ones who assigned partners are told to stand with them, and then the two are pulled apart. What the partners say is stranger than a simple denial. They do not say the worship never happened; they say it was not directed at us. Early scholars explain this as exposing what was actually being served, a projection the worshippers had built and named, so the objects can truthfully deny having received anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing about brokered access for several verses, first by asking whether God could be unaware of such an office, then by describing what happens when the arrangement is examined. This passage supplies the ending. Its audience had a working system of images understood as advocates, and the scene is constructed to show that system from the far side.

keyTerms.note: A command to hold position, the kind given to men lining up before a matter is settled. It fixes both parties in place so the separation that follows can be seen to happen to them.
An intensive form meaning to pull apart what was joined. The bond assumed between worshipper and object is undone as an act, which is why the disowning that follows is not merely spoken.
One who testifies from direct presence, not from report. Offered by the partners as their whole defence, it hands the case to the only party who saw what was actually intended.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian disputes were settled face to face, in front of others. Both sides stood before an arbitrator. Claims were made aloud. Witnesses were produced, or the claim collapsed. The order to stand in your place, the calling of a witness, the sudden parting of two parties: all of it read as court procedure to the first hearers. It was not strange end-of-the-world imagery to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this moment of disowning several times, and the wording changes each time. In one place the idolaters swear they were never idolaters at all. In another, those they called on become their enemies and reject the whole link. Here the denial is sharper than either. Not that it did not happen, but that they were not the ones receiving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is shown to depend on what the worshipper meant. It does not depend on the object placed in front of them. That makes misdirected devotion a private build, not a relationship. And it explains why the objects can deny it honestly. The scene also removes the last comfort of company. Being gathered together turns out to be the setting where everyone is separated. Each case is taken alone.

crossReferences.why: Stages the same confrontation, with the idolaters swearing they had never been idolaters at all.
Says those invoked are heedless of the prayers, and become enemies to their worshippers when gathered.
States that what they took as honour will reject their worship and turn against them.
