studies.applyIt: Bring to mind something you rely on that could not, if asked, confirm that it ever agreed to hold you up. A reputation, a plan, an idea of how your life will go. Say plainly to yourself what it can and cannot actually do. Doing that now is considerably cheaper than doing it later.
studies.explainEasier: On that Day God will gather everyone. He will tell those who worshipped other things to stand with them. Then those things will say: you were not really worshipping us, and God knows it.

studies.title: What It Sent Ahead
studies.meaning: Three things happen in one line. Every soul comes to know by experience what it had sent on ahead, rather than being told about it. Everyone is returned to God, described here with a title that quietly settles the argument the surah has been running, since He is called their real master and the others were not. And the inventions simply go missing. The verb for that is not refutation but desertion: the claims wander off and are not there when needed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the scene in which those who assigned partners are set beside them and separated. The surah has been dismantling brokered access for several passages, and this is where the ledger is opened instead. No occasion is reported for it. The setting is the general Meccan dispute over whether anything follows death at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb of trying something to find out what it really is, as metal is tested. Knowledge here arrives through undergoing rather than through being informed, which is what makes the moment unbearable.
From the vocabulary of paying in advance on a purchase. Deeds are treated as a sum already forwarded to a destination, so what is met later was dispatched earlier by the person meeting it.
The word covers the protector, the freed slave's patron and the ally, a relationship of belonging in both directions. Attaching the word for truth to it declares every rival claim to that role void.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Paying in advance was a familiar contract in Mecca. A buyer paid now for dates or hides to be handed over after the harvest. The whole deal rested on the seller being reliable across months. Caravan backers did the same on a larger scale. They handed over money and waited two seasons to see what came back. The wording of this ayah is drawn straight from that ledger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for sending ahead occurs twice in the Quran. Here it describes every soul without exception meeting what it forwarded. The other place uses it warmly, addressed to those given their record in the right hand and told to eat and drink for what they sent on in days gone by. One word covers both outcomes, with only the tone changing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes the gap between a deed and its result. They are the same thing, seen at two moments. Nothing is added to a person at the end. What was sent is what arrives. That turns the whole idea of reckoning into recognition rather than sentencing. Calling God the true master in the middle of this also answers the surah's long argument about go-betweens. It does so with one word rather than another proof.

crossReferences.why: Describes every soul finding its good presented, and wishing distance from the evil it did.
States the same knowledge in six words: each soul knows what it advanced and what it deferred.
Shows the record leaving out nothing small or large, and everything done found present.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did this week that nobody saw and that will not come back to you. A kindness, or a shortcut. Sit with the idea that it has been sent somewhere rather than ended. You do not need to feel anything dramatic about it. Simply stop treating unobserved actions as though they did not leave.
studies.explainEasier: On that Day every person will meet what they sent ahead of them. Everyone goes back to God, who is their real master. The things they made up will not be there to help.

studies.title: Who Provides From Sky And Earth
studies.meaning: Five questions are put, and the people being questioned supply the answer. Who feeds you from above and below. Who owns your hearing and your sight. Who brings the living out of the dead, and the dead out of the living. Who runs the whole affair. They say God, and the argument is over. What is left is the conclusion, and it is a caution rather than a doctrine. Early scholars note the method. Nothing new is taught here. A gap is simply shown between what the objectors already grant and how they live.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience did not deny God. A supreme creator was granted across the peninsula, and named in oaths and poetry before Islam. That is exactly why the questions can be asked with confidence about the answer. What was in dispute was whether granting it carried any consequences. The surah keeps pressing on that seam, rather than arguing about whether God exists.

keyTerms.note: The root covers anything a creature is given to live on, food, rain, knowledge, a livelihood. It always implies a giver, so the noun cannot be used of something simply present in the world.
Ownership carrying the right of disposal, the root behind the words for king and kingdom. Applied to your own hearing and sight, it makes the most intimate faculties something held on loan.
To handle a matter with its end in view, from the word for the back or rear of a thing. The surah opened with this same verb, so the last question here returns to its first claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Provision in Mecca came from two directions, and both were visible. Rain fell rarely and mattered enormously. What the ground gave up came through wells sunk by earlier generations. The most famous of them stood inside the sanctuary itself. A merchant's year was a bet on both. So when this ayah names the sky and the earth as the sources, it names the two things every household already watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of hearing in the singular with sight in the plural, exactly as it stands here, occurs five times in the Quran. Classical grammarians remarked on how steady the pattern is across every case. Here the pair sits between provision and the running of the universe. So the powers by which a person takes in the world are listed among things owned by someone else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats belief as a matter of consequences, not of information. If the answers people give under questioning are the true ones, then the real question is why nothing follows from them. Naming hearing and sight among what God owns also cuts close. Those were the very tools the objectors were using to test the claim. The conclusion asked for is wariness. That is where knowledge turns into a way of living.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same method, a question the objectors answer themselves, followed by a call to reflect.
Asks who created the heavens and regulated sun and moon, and records the answer as God.
Poses the same question about a creator who provides from the heaven and the earth.

studies.applyIt: Answer the ayah's second question honestly today. Close your eyes for thirty seconds in the middle of something ordinary, then open them. Nothing about that faculty was arranged by you, and it will be withdrawn at a time you do not choose. Let that be a fact you have actually noticed rather than one you agree with.
studies.explainEasier: Ask people who gives them food from the sky and the earth. Ask who owns their ears and eyes, and who runs everything. They answer: God. Then they are told to be careful.

studies.title: Beyond The Truth
studies.meaning: A conclusion is drawn from answers the objectors have just given themselves. The one they named is your Lord, and He is called the Real. Then a question with no middle ground: past the truth, what is left except straying. Early scholars note that the name used here is not simply a claim of accuracy but a statement about what actually exists, so alternatives are not rival truths but absences. The second ayah closes the case by saying the verdict has already settled on those who broke out of bounds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on five questions the audience answered correctly. The surah has been building toward this moment for several verses. Now it takes the step the objectors would not. Nothing is reported about a particular occasion. The setting is a city that granted there was a creator, priced that at nothing, and carried on as before.

keyTerms.note: The root covers what is established, what is due, and what genuinely exists. Used as a name it says God is not merely truthfully described but is the thing everything else is measured against.
From the verb for losing your way or losing an object in the sand. It names disorientation rather than a rival position, which is why the ayah offers no third option between the two.
The root describes a date leaving its skin, so it pictures stepping outside a boundary rather than failing inside one. The word implies there was a shell to be within before it was left.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Navigation across open country was a matter of true bearings. A guide fixed on a star or a known ridge, and there were not several correct routes to a well, only the one and every other direction. Losing the line meant the water was not somewhere else; it was nowhere. The desert supplied this ayah's logic long before anyone applied it to belief.
studies.didYouKnow: Two other places in the Quran use almost this exact sentence. Both say that God is the Real, and that what people call on besides Him is false. Both close with two names of greatness. Here the wording turns instead into a question put to the listener. That places the same claim inside an argument the audience has already half granted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming God as the Real makes truth a matter of what exists. It is not about which opinion has better backing. On that reading the alternatives are not weaker accounts of reality. They are cut loose from it. That explains the sharpness of the question. The next ayah adds something harder: a settled outcome for those who have gone outside the boundary. The passage holds both together without softening either.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing directly, that God is the Reality and what they invoke besides Him is vanity.
Repeats the formula almost word for word, ending on two names of exaltation and supremacy.
Later in this surah the question is asked outright, is it true, and answered with an oath.

studies.applyIt: Pick one belief you hold about your own life that you have never actually tested. That a certain fear is realistic, that someone will not forgive you, that you are past a certain point. Ask yourself once, plainly, whether it is true. Not whether it feels true. The ayah's question is simply whether a thing is real, and it is worth asking at that scale.
studies.explainEasier: God is your Lord, and He is the Real. Anything past the truth is just being lost. So the word of your Lord came true against those who broke away and would not believe.

studies.title: Can Any Of Yours Begin
studies.meaning: A question is put and then answered in the same breath, without waiting. Early scholars note the device. The objectors are given no room to reply, because there is no reply available. Their silence would be the argument. What is asked about is the pair of acts the surah opened with: starting creation, and doing it again. The closing word is not anger but puzzlement. It asks how a person gets turned around while holding the right answer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The images at the sanctuary were credited with speaking up for people and with influence. They were never credited with making anything, and their keepers would not have claimed otherwise. So the question lands on ground the audience shared. This is the second time in thirty verses that the surah has used the pair of verbs for starting and repeating. The first time it was a statement, not a challenge.

keyTerms.note: From a root for sharing a property or a business venture. The possessive ending is pointed: they are described as belonging to the people who named them, which quietly settles who assigned the role.
To bring something back to a state it held before, from the root for returning and for a recurring festival. It makes resurrection a second performance rather than a different kind of act.

A passive verb for being twisted from a direction, used elsewhere of ground overturned. Being passive, it asks what is doing the turning, since the ayah has just shown the person's own answer pointing straight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Partnership was the ordinary shape of Meccan business. A caravan was paid for in shares. Profits were divided by agreement, and what each partner put in was known and stated. Nobody could claim a share without having put something in. Using that language of the idols made a demand the audience understood exactly. Name what they put in, and the account settles itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of beginning creation with repeating it runs through the Quran as a compact argument for resurrection. It appears in surahs of very different lengths and periods. One passage cuts it to four words, saying simply that He begins and repeats. This surah uses it twice. First as a plain statement about God, then as a question nobody in the audience could answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by asking what a claimed power has ever done. It does not try to disprove it. That standard travels well, and the passage applies it to the one act nobody can fake or narrate. Ending on puzzlement rather than condemning is deliberate. The problem described is not ignorance. It is a gap between what a person knows and where they turn, which is harder to account for.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about beginning and repeating, then demands evidence for any other god.
States the two acts plainly and adds the return, without the challenge form used here.
Opens this surah's argument with the same pair of verbs, as a promise rather than a question.

studies.applyIt: Take something you rely on for security and ask what it has actually produced for you, listing items rather than feelings. A job, a network, a savings account. The point is not to find them worthless; most of them have delivered something real. It is to notice which of them you have credited with more than its record supports.
studies.explainEasier: Ask them if any of their so-called partners can start creation and then bring it back. God starts creation and brings it back. So people should not be turned away from Him.

studies.title: Or One Who Must Be Led
studies.meaning: The question narrows from making things to showing the way, and the second half sharpens it into a comparison anyone can settle. On one side, someone who guides to the truth. On the other, someone who cannot find the way himself unless he is led to it. Early scholars note that the second description is not an insult but a definition, and that it applies to every candidate the objectors could name. The closing line asks not what they believe but how they are reaching their judgements at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after a question about who begins and repeats creation. The surah is working through the functions a deity would have to perform, taking them one at a time. Guidance is the second, and it matters more to the argument than power does, because the audience was being asked to follow something. No particular occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: The root behind both the guide on a road and the gift given to a traveller. Guidance in this word is something handed over, which is why the ayah can ask whether a candidate has anything to hand.

A comparative from the word for what is real and what is due. The question is therefore about entitlement rather than preference, asking who has the standing to be followed, not who is more appealing.

From the root for restraining and for wise judgement, the same one behind the word applied to this Book in the surah's first verse. The closing question examines the audience's reasoning, not their conclusion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hiring a guide across the northern route was a decision with a simple test attached. Either the man had crossed it and knew where the water sat, or he had not. Nobody chose a guide by reputation alone or out of loyalty to his family, because the desert settled such questions quickly and permanently. This ayah applies the same hiring standard to the objects people were following.
studies.didYouKnow: The word at the end of this ayah for judging shares its root with the word used of the Book in the surah's opening line. There it is translated as wise. So the surah begins by calling the scripture firmly judged. And it closes this argument by asking the objectors how they judge. The same root frames both ends of the exchange.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is treated as the deciding quality, rather than power. That shifts what is at stake. A being that cannot show the way is no use in the one respect that matters to a person deciding how to live. It may be impressive in other ways. The last question also assumes people answer for their reasoning, not only for their conclusions. A judgement reached badly is itself something to answer for.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same incapacity, those called to guidance who neither hear nor see though they look.
Asks whether most of them hear or understand, after describing someone who took desire as a god.
Says that whomever God leaves astray has no guide at all, the other side of this comparison.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose opinion changes what you do. Ask what qualifies them, concretely, in the area where you follow them. Sometimes the answer is good and you will feel steadier for having checked. Sometimes you will find you have been following someone because they are nearby, which is exactly the test this ayah proposes.
studies.explainEasier: Ask them if any of their partners can lead people to the truth. God leads people to the truth. It makes more sense to follow the one who leads than one who needs leading.

studies.title: Assumption Against The Truth
studies.meaning: A diagnosis is offered in place of an accusation. What most of them follow is not a false doctrine. It is a way of holding beliefs, namely guesswork. Then a general rule is stated in six words of Arabic. A guess cannot stand in for the truth, however firmly it is held. Early scholars are careful here. The target is not thinking or reasoning, which the Quran asks for again and again. The target is the habit of treating a guess as settled. The closing clause adds that the conduct which follows is fully known.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The religious inheritance the audience defended rested on ancestral practice rather than on any claimed revelation, and the Quran elsewhere records them saying so plainly. This ayah names the epistemology behind that defence. It sits in a run of arguments about who creates and who guides, and it explains why those arguments were not landing.

keyTerms.note: A leaning of the mind short of certainty, which can be reasonable or baseless. The Quran uses it both ways, so the fault here is not the state itself but treating it as though it were knowledge.
From the root for wealth and being free of need. The verb asks whether a thing covers a requirement, so the claim is that supposition does not pay for what only truth can settle.
An intensive form of the word for knowledge, placed at the end of an ayah about guessing. The contrast is structural: their supposition is set directly against His complete knowledge of what they do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on estimates. A buyer judged a hide by feel. A season's yield was judged by rumour from returning riders, and a partner was judged by his name. Everyone knew the difference between a good estimate and a checked fact. Everyone knew which one you could stake a caravan on. Divining arrows kept at the sanctuary were used for choices nobody could estimate. That is the exact practice this word of the ayah describes.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that a guess is no substitute for the truth appears twice in the Quran, in nearly the same words. In the other place it follows a statement that the names people gave their gods were invented. Those names carried no authority from God. Both places attach the same diagnosis to the same practice, several surahs apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the quality of a belief part of its moral standing. Holding something without warrant is treated as a failure, not just as a weak piece of thinking. That raises the cost of comfortable assumptions a great deal. It also implies that the truth can be reached. The criticism would be empty otherwise. Certainty is not demanded. What is refused is the pretence of it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same principle almost word for word, that assumptions are no substitute for truth.
Forbids pursuing what you have no knowledge of, and says hearing, sight and mind are questioned.
Warns that following most people leads astray, since they follow assumption and only conjecture.

studies.applyIt: Catch one thing today that you say with confidence and have never checked. A statistic, a claim about someone's motives, a piece of advice you repeat. Look it up, or admit out loud that you do not actually know. Doing this once is uncomfortable in a way that tells you how much of your talking is estimate.
studies.explainEasier: Most people only follow their own guesses. A guess does not help at all against the truth. It cannot take the place of what is real. And God knows exactly what they do.

studies.title: Confirming What Came Before
studies.meaning: Two positive claims replace a denial. This recitation confirms what stood in front of it. And it sets out the Book in detail. Early scholars divide over that second phrase. Some read it as the detailing of earlier scriptures. Others read it as the unfolding of a divine record from which revelations are drawn. The sources keep both. The argument is that a forgery would not do this work. It would not back rival documents, or take on the load of explaining them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Jewish and Christian communities were known in Arabia through trade with Yemen, Syria and the settlements north of Mecca. Their scriptures were part of the general landscape, even where the details were vague. So the claim to confirm rather than replace was something people could check. It was not a slogan. The Quran makes it again and again, in Meccan and in later passages.

keyTerms.note: Passive of the verb for cutting and stitching something into shape. Denying the possibility rather than the fact is stronger: the claim is that a text doing this work could not have been assembled by anyone.
From the root for truthfulness. It means declaring something true and standing behind it, not merely agreeing with it, which is why the word carries a risk the forger would avoid.
To separate a joined thing at its natural joints, the word a butcher or a tailor would use. Applied to a book it means laying out what was folded, section by section rather than in summary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Documents were rare and heavy in Arabia. Written scripture belonged to settled communities with scribes and libraries. A Meccan merchant met it as something other people owned, in cities he visited. That distance is part of the setting. The audience knew such books existed. They knew the books were long. And they knew that nobody among them was placed to have copied one.
studies.didYouKnow: The claim to confirm earlier scripture appears across surahs from very different periods, and it never varies. One passage states it while calling the earlier book a model and a mercy. Another places the Quran as confirming what came before and standing as a measure over it. That steadiness is itself unusual. A text given over twenty-three years had many chances to drop an awkward position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as one continuing project. It is not a set of unrelated announcements. That changes how a reader holds earlier scriptures, and what newness can mean here. The passage claims to extend and explain, not to replace one book with another. It also stakes the credibility of the Quran on a link it did not have to claim. That is the shape the argument from unlikelihood takes here.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same three phrases, not a fabricated tale but a confirmation and a detailing.
States the relationship fully, revealed with truth, confirming the scripture that preceded it.
Names the earlier book directly and calls this one a confirming Book in the Arabic language.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran today. Look only for the places where it assumes you know something already: a name, an event, an earlier promise. You will find several on almost any page. Notice that the Book is speaking into a conversation that was running before it arrived. That is exactly what it says about itself.
studies.explainEasier: This Quran could not have been made up by anyone but God. It agrees with the books that came before it. It explains them in full. It comes from the Lord of all the worlds.

studies.title: Produce A Single Chapter
studies.meaning: The charge of invention is answered with an invitation rather than a defence. Produce one chapter of the same kind, and bring in whoever you can to help. Early scholars note two features of the wording. The unit named is small, the shortest surahs running to a few lines, so the bar is set low rather than high. And assistance is explicitly permitted, which removes the excuse that the challenge was aimed at one person's talent against another's.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabic poetry was the high art of the peninsula, and its contest sport. It was judged in public at seasonal fairs. The leading families of Mecca included men known for fine speech. So the challenge went out to a culture equipped to answer it, and keen to. Similar challenges appear elsewhere in the Quran at other scales. The passages around them record no attempt that satisfied the audience itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb for cutting and stitching material into a finished object, with the pronoun attached. The accusation is not error but manufacture, which is why the reply asks them to manufacture something comparable.
The word for a section of the Quran, connected by the classical lexicographers to a wall's course or an enclosure. Its use here sets the unit of the challenge, and the shortest are only a few lines.
The ordinary verb for calling someone to your aid. Including it turns a personal contest into an open one, since the objectors are told to bring in every helper available to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry contests were public events with real stakes. A tribe could rise in standing on the strength of one ode. Famous pieces were memorised across the peninsula by men who never wrote anything down. Reciters travelled with their material. Audiences knew the difference between good verse and the other kind. So a challenge to produce speech of that quality was aimed at specialists.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran issues this challenge at more than one scale. One passage asks for a single chapter and calls the audience's witnesses. Another asks for ten invented chapters. A third states that all people and jinn together could not produce the like of it, even working with one another. The unit asked for varies. The terms of the invitation stay the same.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage stakes the claim of revelation on something the public can test. It does not rest on private experience. That is unusual, and risky, since a successful reply would have settled the matter. It also implies that the difference between this speech and other speech is meant to be heard. That puts the reader in the seat of a judge rather than a spectator. And it makes close listening part of what is being asked.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the challenge for those in doubt, asking for one chapter and calling their witnesses.
Raises the demand to ten invented chapters, with the same permission to call in whoever they can.
States the outcome as a claim, that people and jinn together could not produce its like.

studies.applyIt: Read a short surah aloud today. Use Arabic if you can, or translation if you cannot. Then read aloud a paragraph of any writing you admire. Do not try to reach a verdict. Just notice that the ayah expects the comparison to be made with your own ears, rather than accepted on authority.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said he made the Quran up. The answer was simple. Let them write just one chapter like it, and let them ask anyone they want for help.

studies.title: Denying What They Have Not Grasped
studies.meaning: The refusal is located precisely. They rejected something they had not gone all the way around. Its outcome had not yet arrived either. Early scholars divide over that second phrase. Some read it as the explanation they had not waited for. Others read it as the events the warnings pointed to, which had not yet happened. Either way the fault is timing, not reasoning. A verdict was returned before the evidence was complete. The passage notes that earlier peoples made exactly the same error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just issued a challenge to produce a matching chapter. This ayah explains why the challenge went unmet, in a different sense. The rejection had already happened, before anyone examined anything. The closing instruction is to look at what became of earlier wrongdoers. As elsewhere in this surah, that points to ruins along the trade routes its audience travelled.

keyTerms.note: To go all the way around something, as a wall encircles a garden. Knowledge in this image is not a glance but a circuit, which sets a demanding standard for anyone issuing a final judgement.
From a root meaning to return to an origin. The classical readings run from the explanation of a saying to the event a warning finally resolves into, and both senses are preserved in the sources.
From the word for a heel, so it names what comes behind rather than what is planned. It describes results as they actually arrive, which is why the ayah asks the reader to look rather than to reason.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Judgement was normally held back until a caravan returned. A merchant could not tell for months whether a season had gone well. Everyone had watched confident predictions collapse when the riders finally came in. Waiting for the outcome before pronouncing on it was ordinary business sense in Mecca. That makes the haste this ayah describes a break from the audience's own practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this charge at the point of reckoning. There the question put to people is whether they rejected the signs without taking them in. That question uses the same verb of encompassing that appears here. So the charge is not developed over time. It is stated at the beginning and repeated at the end, in the same terms.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Humility is given a precise content here. It is the recognition that a judgement can outrun its evidence. That is not an argument for holding off every conclusion, since the passage itself concludes. It is an argument about order. Denial is a claim, and it needs as much warrant as agreement does. The reference to earlier peoples then adds something. Time settles some questions on its own, whether or not anyone was willing to wait.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same charge as a question at the reckoning, rejecting signs without comprehending them.
States the rule this ayah's failure breaks, not pursuing what you have no knowledge of.
Shows the same audience listening yet unable to take it in, dismissing it as tales of the ancients.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you dismiss something within a few seconds of hearing it. A book, a proposal, an explanation from someone you disagree with. Give it a full minute before deciding, and say out loud what you would need to know to judge it properly. Usually the list is longer than you expected.
studies.explainEasier: They said no to something they had not really understood yet. They had not waited to see how it would turn out. People before them did the same thing, and it did not end well.

studies.title: Some Of Them Believe
studies.meaning: An audience is divided into two plain groups and no explanation is offered for the split. Some believe in it, some do not, and the sentence stops there. What follows is not a verdict on the second group but a statement about knowledge: your Lord knows best who the corrupters are. Early scholars read the ending as narrowing the charge, since not everyone who withholds belief is described that way. The one being addressed is left with a mixed result and no obligation to sort it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch where the surah keeps turning from argument to the messenger's own situation. Some in Mecca had accepted the message quietly, several of them from leading families. Others had hardened. The passage describes that mixture rather than reporting an incident. It belongs to a set of ayat that console a man watching people he had known all his life divide over something he could not make them see.

keyTerms.note: A partitive phrase repeated twice in one short ayah, once for each group. The repetition holds the two apart without ranking them, and it keeps both inside the same word for the people.
A comparative form, so the claim is not simply that God knows but that He knows better than the one being addressed. It quietly removes the messenger from the role of assessor.
From a root for something going rotten or a thing breaking down. It names damage done rather than belief withheld, which is why it applies to a narrower group than the ayah's second half.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had a small population, locked together by marriage. So division over the message ran through households rather than between them. A man might have a brother who accepted it. He might have a wife who did not, and a business partner who had not decided. There was no separate place for either group to go. Everyone went on sharing wells, markets and funerals with people whose stand on this had become the largest fact about them.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact division of an audience appears elsewhere in the Quran, in nearly the same words. It describes people among whom some believed in it and some held back. The surah uses the same construction three times in three ayat in a row. First for belief, then for those who listen, then for those who look. It builds a small catalogue of ways to be present without arriving.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering for outcomes is separated from answering for effort. Someone can deliver a message faithfully and watch it divide people. The passage does not treat that as failure. Leaving the judgement of who is truly destructive to God also guards the believer against one temptation. That is the slide from disagreeing with people to filing them. Knowing better is presented as God's role, and it is not handed on.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same division of an audience, some who believed in it and some who held back.
Later in this surah, the same point is made as a question about compelling people to believe.
States the limit of the role directly, a reminder to give, with no controlling authority over anyone.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone close to you who has not come to where you are, in faith or in anything else. Notice whether you have started keeping a private file on their motives. Set it down for a week. You can keep hoping and keep talking without also holding the verdict, and this ayah takes the verdict off you.
studies.explainEasier: Some of the people believe in this message. Some of them do not believe in it. Your Lord knows best which of them are really out to cause harm.

studies.title: I Have My Deeds
studies.meaning: The instruction for being called a liar is not a counter-argument. It is a sentence that separates two accounts without insult. Each party owns its own actions, and neither answers for what the other does. Early scholars note that this is a stepping back rather than a truce. Nothing is conceded about who is right. What it removes is the tangle. No further exchange is needed, and the speaker walks away holding only his own record.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the period when calling him a liar had become the standard public position. It was no longer an occasional insult. The passage sits among several that address the messenger's own conduct under pressure. Similar formulas appear elsewhere in the Quran. One whole surah ends on the same separation. They belong to this stage rather than to the later years.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so it means repeatedly declaring someone false rather than doubting once. The intensity is in the verb itself, which is why the reply it prompts is notable for its flatness.
The everyday word for labour and action, not for belief or intention. Framing the separation around deeds rather than doctrines keeps the sentence to something both sides can actually see.
From the root for recovery from illness and for clearing a debt. It names being released from liability, which is exactly what the sentence does for each side with respect to the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Liability in Arabia was shared by default. A clan answered for the debts and blood claims of its members. A family could be pursued for what one man had done. Clearing yourself in public of responsibility for another was a recognised act with real consequences. This ayah borrows that legal move and applies it to conduct rather than blood. It would have sounded precise rather than resigned.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this separation in several forms across different surahs. One passage has believers say it after hearing idle talk, adding peace upon you. Another places nearly the same words in a longer instruction that ends by saying God will bring us together. And the shortest surah of its kind closes with a single line dividing two ways without any argument at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a boundary that protects both the message and the messenger. Not every rejection needs an answer. Going on arguing can itself become a way of accepting the other side's terms. Making deeds the unit of separation also carries a claim. What a person finally answers for is their own action. No accusation and no association can transfer that.

crossReferences.why: Has believers say the same words after hearing vain talk, and add a greeting of peace.
Places the identical phrase inside a longer instruction that ends with God bringing everyone together.
Closes a whole surah on the same separation, stated in its shortest possible form.

studies.applyIt: Find one running argument you keep re-entering with someone who is not going to change. Decide, before it starts again, on a single sentence that ends your part without insulting them. Then use it. The point is not to win the exchange or to concede it, only to stop carrying what belongs to the other side.
studies.explainEasier: If they call you a liar, say this. I have my own deeds and you have yours. You are not to blame for what I do, and I am not to blame for what you do.

studies.title: Listening Without Hearing
studies.meaning: Two groups are described doing everything correctly on the outside. Some listen, some watch, and both questions that follow assume the effort was real. What is missing is named by two clauses: they do not use their minds, they do not see. Early scholars read the deafness and blindness as figures for a faculty gone unused rather than absent. The third ayah then rules out the reading this could invite, stating that no one is deprived by God and that people do this to themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The message was recited publicly at the sanctuary and at the seasonal fairs, so opponents heard it constantly and some are reported to have listened privately at night. This passage describes that situation exactly: an audience with full access and no result. The final ayah closes off the objection that such an outcome would make God responsible for it.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for hearing that adds effort and intention, meaning to seek out the sound. The word concedes that the attention was genuine, which is what makes the outcome worth explaining.
The root also describes something solid with no opening, as a rock or a sealed vessel. The image is of sound arriving at a surface with nowhere to enter, rather than of a damaged ear.
From a root for darkness and for putting something out of its proper place. Repeating the verb for both halves of the ayah lets one word deny the charge against God and land it on people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry and news travelled by ear in Arabia. Audiences were trained listeners who could hold a long ode after one hearing. Being able to repeat something back was no proof of having accepted it. Everyone knew the difference between two kinds of listener. One man learned a rival's verse in order to answer it. Another was moved by it. The distinction this passage draws was familiar in that culture's own listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran repeats this pair of images with small variations. One passage describes people who have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with and ears they do not hear with. Another puts the same two questions to the messenger about the deaf and the blind. The images stay constant while the surrounding argument changes, which suggests a fixed diagnosis rather than a metaphor chosen for effect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Access and reception are separated. Hearing a thing is no guarantee of receiving it. That moves the deciding factor from information to something inside the listener. The third ayah then guards against fatalism with unusual directness. It insists that God wrongs no one in the least. Whatever was closed was closed from the inside. The passage puts the whole weight of that outcome on the person.

crossReferences.why: Spells out the same three faculties present and unused, hearts, eyes and ears that do not work.
Puts the identical two questions to the messenger about making the deaf hear and guiding the blind.
States the same conclusion, that God did not wrong them but they used to wrong their own souls.

studies.applyIt: Recall something true you were told years before you were able to take it in. By a parent, a teacher, someone who has since died. Notice that the words were complete at the time and you were not. Then consider what you are currently hearing correctly and receiving nothing from, and hold that question open rather than answering it.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them listen to you, but they do not really hear. Some of them look at you, but they do not really see. God does not wrong people at all. They wrong themselves.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Only An Hour Of Day
studies.meaning: Two details do the work. The whole span before the gathering will feel like part of a single daytime hour. And people will recognise one another. So who they are survives, even as the length of time collapses. Early scholars differ over what is shortened. Some say life in the world, others the interval before rising. The sources record both without deciding. The loss named at the end is specific: those who denied the meeting, and who never came under guidance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The objection this answers was not moral but temporal, since the audience found the idea of a delayed reckoning implausible over long stretches of time. The surah has already described earlier generations removed and their ground handed on. Here the same span is measured from the other end, where it turns out to be short. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb for driving a scattered group together into one place, used of herding and of mustering an army. It implies people brought in from separate directions rather than assembling themselves.
Any brief stretch rather than a fixed sixty minutes. The same word names the final Hour elsewhere in the Quran, so a term for the shortest interval also names the longest-awaited event.
A reciprocal form of the verb for knowing, so the recognition runs both ways. It preserves the ordinary social world at the very moment the passage compresses all its time to nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was measured by shadow, by the stages of a journey, and by the season of a caravan. It was never measured by a clock. An hour of the day was a working unit. It was roughly what it took to water a herd or reach the next rise. So the comparison in this ayah named something quite precise to its first hearers. The whole of history is cut down to one small errand.
studies.didYouKnow: Several passages describe this shortening, and none of them agree on the figure. That is the point. In one, the sinners swear they stayed only an hour. In another it seems like an evening or a morning. In a third they murmur ten days, before the most exact among them says one. The estimates disagree because the experience is being described as unreliable, not measured.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Length of time is treated as a feature of experience, not as a fixed quantity. That undercuts an argument built on how long things take. If a whole life can shrink to an hour in hindsight, then the delay that made the reckoning seem unreal is not a stable fact about the world. Recognition surviving that squeeze matters too. People arrive as themselves, known to one another. They are not dissolved into a crowd.

crossReferences.why: Has the sinners swear they stayed only an hour, and calls that estimate a delusion.
Records the same disagreement over how long, from ten days down to a single day.
Uses the same measure, an hour of a day, and joins it to an instruction to be patient.

studies.applyIt: Think back to a period of your life that felt endless while you were inside it. A school year, an illness, a job you needed to leave. Notice how much space it occupies now, which is usually a paragraph. Then look at the week ahead and see whether anything in it deserves quite the weight you are giving it.
studies.explainEasier: On the Day God gathers everyone, it will feel like they only stayed an hour of one day. They will know each other. Those who denied meeting God will have lost everything.

studies.title: Whether We Show You
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are named and then made equal. The messenger may live to see part of what was promised. Or he may be taken first. Either way, the return is to God. Early scholars note that the sentence is addressed to a man who might reasonably want to see it come true in his lifetime. It declines to promise him that. What is guaranteed instead is the outcome itself, and the fact that everything they do is witnessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from years when nothing visible was changing. The community was small and hard pressed. Warnings had been given and no consequence had arrived. Other passages give the same instruction in almost identical words. One of them adds directly that the duty is to deliver, and the reckoning belongs to God. That is the division this ayah assumes.

keyTerms.note: A causative form with an emphatic ending, so it means We definitely make you see. The certainty sits on the showing rather than on whether it happens in this life, which is left open.
From the root for paying a debt in full. Death in this word is a complete collection rather than a loss, which is why the Quran uses it for the taking of a soul in several places.
One who testifies from having been there. Placed at the end, it answers the worry the ayah raises: even if the messenger does not see the outcome, nothing about the matter goes unobserved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long projects in that world often outlived the men who began them. A well dug for a clan served grandchildren. A feud opened in one generation was settled in another. A caravan route was built up over decades by families, not by single men. Starting something you would not see finished was an ordinary part of life. It was not a special hardship kept for prophets.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this pair of possibilities to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) at least three times, in three different surahs, in nearly the same words. One version adds that his duty is only to deliver the message. Another says that vengeance will be taken either way. The repetition suggests a question that kept coming back, not one raised on a single occasion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being proved right is separated from the mission. A person can complete their task fully and never see the result. The passage treats that as an ordinary arrangement, not a disappointment. That changes how effort is valued. The work is finished when it is done, not when it is confirmed. Naming God as witness supplies the only thing actually needed. The record exists whether or not anyone living sees it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two possibilities and divides the roles, delivery for him and reckoning for God.
Repeats the pair almost word for word, joined to an instruction to be patient with the promise.
Addresses the community's dependence on seeing him present, and what should not change if he dies.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are working on that will probably not be finished by you: raising someone, a slow repair in a relationship, work at a job that outlasts your tenure. Do the next small piece of it this week without checking for progress. That is the exact posture the ayah is describing, and it is available at any scale.
studies.explainEasier: God may let you see part of what He promised them. Or He may take you first. Either way, they all come back to Him. And God sees everything they do.

studies.title: Every Community Has One
studies.meaning: A rule is stated with no exceptions attached. Each community receives a messenger. Once he has come, the case between them is settled fairly, and nobody is treated unjustly. Early scholars note that the arrival of the messenger is what makes judgement possible. So the order is not decoration. The next line gives the objectors' response. It is impatience rather than argument. They ask when, and the question is quoted without being answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew of earlier peoples through the ruins on their trade routes and through stories exchanged with Jewish and Christian traders. Setting out a universal rule met a specific worry, that this message was a local novelty. Elsewhere the Quran states the same principle in different words, and once tells the audience to travel through the earth and see how it turned out for the deniers.

keyTerms.note: Any group bound by something shared, whether descent, place or way of life. The word is deliberately loose, which lets the rule cover peoples the audience had never heard of as easily as their own.
A passive from the root for completing and adjudicating a matter. Leaving the verb passive keeps attention on the settlement rather than on the judge, and implies the outcome is already fixed.

A commitment to something at a set time, used in the Quran for both reward and reckoning. The objectors use the word themselves, which means they are demanding delivery of something they say is not coming.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was the peninsula's justice. Two parties agreed on a judge, often a man from a neutral clan with a reputation for fairness, and the hearing could not begin until he was present and both sides had stated their case. Judgement without a hearing was not thought of as harsh; it was thought of as void. The sequence this ayah describes was the ordinary shape of a fair settlement.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this principle in several forms and never softens it. One passage says a messenger was sent to every community with the same instruction. Another says there is no community through which a warner has not passed. A third says God never punishes until a messenger has been sent. Three surahs of different periods carry the same rule, with nothing added to soften it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is made to depend on prior notice. That is a claim about God's method rather than about human deserving, and it removes a whole class of objections about people who never heard. It also raises the standing of prophecy from a favour granted to some peoples to a condition of fairness for all of them. The fairness named at the end is not mercy; it is the absence of any wrong being done.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule and tells the audience to travel and see how it ended for the deniers.
Puts it as a negative, that there is no community through which a warner has not passed.
Draws the consequence, that no punishment comes before a messenger has been sent.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you made about someone without hearing them out. A judgement about why they behaved as they did, formed before you asked. Go and ask, if the person is still reachable. If they are not, at least name what you decided without evidence, since that is the exact procedure this ayah rules out.
studies.explainEasier: Every group of people gets a messenger from God. After he comes, God judges them fairly. No one is treated badly. Some people ask when this will happen, if you are telling the truth.

studies.title: No Power Over Myself
studies.meaning: The answer to a taunt about timing begins by conceding more than was asked. He cannot even arrange harm or benefit for himself, except as God wills. So the question of when a promised outcome arrives was never his to answer. Then comes the general rule. Each community has a set term. When it comes, nothing shifts it by an hour in either direction. Early scholars note the balance, since delay is ruled out as firmly as haste.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, right after the objectors demand to know when the promise will be fulfilled. This kind of exchange recurs through the surah. Taunts are met by statements about who decides, not by predictions. A close parallel elsewhere adds that if the messenger knew the unseen he would have secured much good for himself. That makes the same admission in a different form.

keyTerms.note: The verb for owning with the right to dispose, from the root behind king and kingdom. Denying it about his own harm and benefit is the strongest available way of saying he holds no lever at all.
A fixed span with a known end, the word used for the maturity date of a debt. Applied to a whole community it makes a nation's life a term already written rather than an open-ended run.
Paired here with its opposite for bringing something forward. Using both verbs closes the door in both directions, so the term is protected from anxiety as much as from impatience.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Mecca ran to a stated date, and both sides knew what that meant. A creditor could not collect early. A debtor could not push the day back. The term was the contract. Caravan backers lived inside the same discipline, unable to hurry a return or delay a settlement. The wording here is the wording of that agreement, applied to the life of a whole people.
studies.didYouKnow: This declaration of powerlessness is made more than once and in stronger forms elsewhere. One passage has the messenger say he has no control over benefit or harm to himself and that knowing the future would have secured him much good. Another has him say it is not in his power to harm his listeners or to bring them to right conduct. The Quran never softens these statements.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is stripped of the powers people expect it to carry. A messenger delivers, and does not dispose. That protects the message from being judged by what he can produce. It also protects him from claims he cannot meet. The fixed term then answers impatience on both sides at once. Those demanding punishment cannot pull it forward. Those dreading it cannot push it away.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller version, adding that knowledge of the future would have brought him much good.
States the same limit toward others, no power to harm them or bring them to right conduct.
Repeats the rule about a nation's term in almost identical words, in another Meccan surah.

studies.applyIt: Say plainly to yourself one thing you have been trying to control that is not yours. Someone's opinion of you, a diagnosis, the pace of a process. Not as resignation, since the ayah is spoken by a man who kept working. Just name it accurately once. Then notice how much of your effort was going into the part you do not hold.
studies.explainEasier: I cannot even help or harm myself, unless God wills it. Every nation has a set time. When that time comes, they cannot push it back an hour, or pull it forward.

studies.title: Now, After Demanding It
studies.meaning: A question is put back to people who have been calling for a reckoning. Suppose it came, by night or by day. Which part of it were you hoping to hurry. Then the second ayah stages the moment itself. It catches the belief arriving one instant too late, with a single word: now. Early scholars read the sequence as showing that the demand and the faith come from the same source. Neither takes the matter seriously until it is standing in the room.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands to see the threatened punishment are recorded repeatedly in this period, sometimes as taunts and sometimes as genuine challenges. The surah answers them here and returns to the theme later in the account of Pharaoh, who declares belief as the water closes over him and is told the same thing in the same word. That parallel within one surah is deliberate.

keyTerms.note: Specifically an arrival while people are settled for the night, from the word for spending the night somewhere. It names the hour when a raid was most feared, so the term carries dread on its own.

A form that adds asking for to the verb for haste. It describes wanting something brought forward, which is what makes the question so pointed: they are being asked to name the part they wanted early.
The ordinary word for the present instant, carrying an interrogative note here. Standing alone it does the work of a whole argument, marking the exact width of the gap that has been missed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Raids came before dawn. A tribe moved at night and struck a sleeping camp at first light. The whole matter was over before most people were properly awake. Every settlement kept watches for that reason, and the fear was exact rather than general. When this ayah names night and day as the two options, it names the raider's hour first. Then it removes even that much warning.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for now that closes the second ayah carries a questioning edge in Arabic. In that exact form it occurs only twice in the whole Quran. Both occurrences sit in this surah. The second comes forty verses later. It is addressed to Pharaoh at the moment he declares belief, with the water already closing over him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line around when a turn toward God still counts. The line falls at the point where the matter becomes visible. That is not arbitrary. Belief forced by an arriving consequence is not the same act as belief offered while the outcome is still open. One is a choice and the other is a recognition. The question about which part they wanted hastened also shows how little the demand was ever meant seriously.

crossReferences.why: Shows faith declared at the moment of seeing the punishment, and states plainly that it did not help.
Later in this surah, Pharaoh's belief while drowning is answered with the very same word for now.
Has the guilty ask to be sent back, saying they have now seen and heard and are convinced.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change you know you will make eventually, once something forces it. A conversation, a habit, a debt. Do the smallest version of it today rather than at the point where you will have no choice. The whole difference the ayah marks is between an act you chose and the same act after it stopped being optional.
studies.explainEasier: Some people kept asking for the punishment to come. They were asked which part of it they were in a hurry for. When it does come, believing then will be too late.

studies.title: Yes, By My Lord
studies.meaning: A sentence is spoken to those who wronged, and its logic is closed. What is tasted is exactly what was earned. The question is phrased so that no other answer is available. Then the scene shifts back to the present. Someone asks, apparently in earnest, whether it is really true. The reply is an oath. Early scholars note that the messenger is rarely told to swear. The oath here is followed not by an argument but by a plain statement that they cannot get out of the way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question quoted is different in tone from the taunts elsewhere in the surah, and early scholars read it as coming from people genuinely unsettled rather than from opponents scoring a point. That may be why the answer is an oath rather than a proof. Nothing in the classical sources ties it to a named individual, and the surah leaves the questioner unidentified.

keyTerms.note: The verb for taking something in by the tongue, used across the Quran for punishment. It makes the experience direct and personal rather than observed, which no other verb in the passage would do.
From a root for remaining and lasting, used of things that outlive their expected span. As a noun attached to punishment it removes the one thing every hardship in this life carries, an end in sight.
From the root for inability, in a form meaning to render someone else unable. The denial says they cannot put the matter beyond God's reach, whether by flight, argument or delay.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia was not a formality. Men swore by their fathers, by the sanctuary, or by the objects they revered. A broken oath cost a man his name for good. Legal disputes could turn entirely on which party was willing to swear. So being told to swear by one's Lord, and then to add nothing further, was a known way of closing a question rather than continuing it.
studies.didYouKnow: There are exactly three places in the Quran where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told to swear by his Lord. This is one of them. The other two are in later surahs. One is about the coming of the Hour and one about resurrection. All three oaths answer the same doubt. In each case the oath stands in place of further argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats certainty as something that can be stated, not only proved. That is a limited move, made in one narrow class of cases, and the Quran uses it sparingly. Behind it lies the matched wording of the first ayah. There, reward is described as nothing more than what was earned. Together they claim the outcome is neither arbitrary nor open to bargaining. That is why swearing to it costs nothing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same oath formula in answer to those who deny that the Hour will come upon them.
The third instance of the oath, answering those who claim they will not be raised.
Continues the same scene in this surah, with remorse hidden and judgement passed equitably.

studies.applyIt: Notice how rarely you say plainly that you are certain of something. We hedge almost everything, partly out of modesty and partly to keep an exit. Pick one thing you actually believe and say it today without softening it. Then notice whether the hedging you usually add was honesty or only cover.
studies.explainEasier: The wrongdoers will be told to taste a lasting punishment for what they did. People ask if this is really true. The answer is: yes, by my Lord, it is true, and you cannot escape it.

studies.title: Everything On Earth As Ransom
studies.meaning: An imagined case is put and not granted. If a wrongdoing soul owned the whole earth, it would hand that over to buy its way out. This tells you what the moment is worth, rather than what money can do. The next detail is stranger, and easy to pass over. They conceal their remorse. Early scholars offer two readings. They hide it from one another out of shame, or the feeling is so complete that no strength is left to show it. Judgement then falls with equity, and no one is wronged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage that began with the demand to see the punishment hastened. Ransom was an ordinary part of life in Arabia. It was used for captives, for blood claims, and for release from an obligation. So the image would have been read as a legal proposal, not a figure of speech. The Quran uses the same imagined case in several surahs of different periods.

keyTerms.note: From the root for redeeming a captive by payment. The word belongs to a real transaction with an agreed price, which is what makes its refusal here a statement about the kind of debt involved.
The verb for keeping something private. Early scholars read the hiding either as shame before others or as a grief too complete to be expressed, and the sources preserve both without deciding.
Regret over an action once its result is visible, distinct from the word for turning back in repentance. It names the feeling without the movement, which is precisely why it arrives too late here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was a working part of Arabian life. Captives taken in a raid were held for payment in camels, blood claims were settled by negotiated compensation, and a man in debt could be redeemed by his clan. Everyone understood that almost any predicament had a price if enough relatives could be persuaded to meet it. That assumption is the one this ayah takes away.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this imagined case at least three times, and raises the amount each telling. One passage says the earth full of gold would not be accepted. Another says everything on earth, and the like of it again. A third lists a man's children, spouse, brother and sheltering family, before adding everyone else on earth. The sum keeps growing and the answer never changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Some debts are shown to be of a kind that cannot be handed on or paid off. That sets a limit on what wealth is for. It is not a criticism of property. The passage assumes ownership is real and simply notes where its reach ends. The insistence on equity in the same breath matters too. It rules out reading the refusal as harshness. Nothing extra is taken. What is denied is only putting one thing in place of another.

crossReferences.why: States the same offer at a different price, the earth full of gold refused as ransom.
Extends the ransom to family and then to everyone on earth, with the same outcome.
Names the specific limit, that no parent can avail a child and no child a parent, on that Day.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation you fixed with money that you could not have fixed any other way. Now think of one thing in your life that money has never touched: a rift, a regret, someone's absence. Hold both facts at once without resolving them. The ayah is about the boundary between them, and most of us know exactly where it runs.
studies.explainEasier: If a person who did wrong owned the whole earth, they would give it all away to escape. But it will not work. They will hide their regret, and God will judge them fairly.

studies.title: The Promise Is True
studies.meaning: Two announcements are made with the same opening particle. It is a word that halts the sentence and calls for attention before anything is said. First, everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God. Second, His promise is true. Putting ownership before promise is the argument in miniature. A promise is only as good as the resources behind it. Here the resources are everything. The final line adds giving life and causing death, then the return. So the one who guarantees the outcome also arranges the journey to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after a scene of ransom refused and remorse concealed. The surah has been describing the reckoning at length, and this pair of verses steps back from the picture to state the ground it rests on. No occasion is reported. The audience being addressed had already conceded God's ownership of the heavens and the earth, which is why the first announcement is framed as a reminder rather than a claim.

keyTerms.note: A particle that opens a sentence to arrest attention, roughly the force of stopping mid-conversation. Repeating it twice in one ayah marks both statements as things the listener already knows but has not acted on.
A commitment to something at a set time, used in the Quran for both what is hoped and what is feared. The word carries no tone of its own, which is why it fits reward and reckoning equally.
Paired here with its opposite in four Arabic words. The pairing recurs across the Quran as a compact statement of authority over the one boundary no other power in the passage has been able to cross.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in Arabia was backed by what the promiser could visibly command. A man's guarantee was worth his herds and his standing. It was also worth his clan's willingness to back him. Everyone weighed a pledge by that arithmetic before accepting it. A guarantee from someone with nothing behind it was simply not taken. So the order of these two announcements would have read to that audience as a credit check.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that the promise of God is true recurs across the Quran, in surahs of every period. Sometimes it closes a warning. Sometimes it opens a comfort. In one place it is joined to an instruction to be patient, and not to be belittled by those who lack certainty. The same four words serve as the ground for hope and for caution, without changing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hope is given a foundation rather than a feeling. What makes the promise reliable is stated as ownership, and power over life and death. Both are claims about God that can be checked. Neither is encouragement offered to the listener. That keeps hope from resting on mood. The closing note about most people not knowing also implies something. The difficulty is not the strength of the evidence. It is the attention paid to it.

crossReferences.why: Joins the same statement about the promise to patience and to not being belittled by the uncertain.
Sets out the same sequence of life, death, life again and the return, as a question about denial.
States the giving of life and death alongside the command by which anything comes to be.

studies.applyIt: Think of one promise someone kept to you when it would have been easy not to. Recall what made you trust it beforehand. Not their sincerity, probably, but what they could actually do. Then read this pair of verses again in that order, ownership first and promise second. Notice that the reassurance is built the same way.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. What He promises is true, but most people do not know this. He gives life and He takes it, and you will be brought back to Him.

studies.title: Healing For What Is Inside
studies.meaning: Four things are named, and the address narrows as it goes. Counsel arrives for all people, then healing for what is in the chests, then guidance and mercy. The last two are specified for believers. Early scholars note that healing is placed before guidance, so the text is described as treating something before it teaches anything. The next verse then tells people what to be glad about, and weighs it against what they pile up.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely addressed to an audience arguing about where the revelation came from. This passage steps outside that argument to describe what the text does instead. Early scholars record no specific occasion. They read the address to all people as a deliberate widening after a long stretch aimed at opponents.

keyTerms.note: Speech aimed at softening rather than informing, the kind that works on the will. Naming it first places the text's effect before its content, which the sequence of the verse then continues.
The ordinary medical word for recovery from illness. Its object here is what is in the chests, so the trouble being treated is located inside a person rather than in their circumstances.
The Quran uses this for the seat of what a person conceals: doubt, resentment, intention. Naming the chest rather than the heart points at the container rather than at the organ inside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in Arabia was practical and limited. There was cautery, cupping, honey, herbs, and the setting of bones. Illnesses of the chest were understood physically. The words for a cure were familiar to everyone. Using that word for what a recitation does to a person inside borrowed language from a craft the audience trusted. It applied that language to something nobody could see.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes itself as healing in several places. The descriptions always carry a limit. One passage calls it healing and mercy for believers, while adding nothing but loss for wrongdoers. Another calls it guidance and healing for those who believe, and something quite different for those who do not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as treatment before instruction. That assumes a particular diagnosis. The obstacle to guidance is not a lack of information but something lodged inside a person. That explains how the same text can be read by two people with opposite results. The next verse then moves joy. It shifts it from what has been gathered to what has been given, and it does so by command rather than by argument.

crossReferences.why: Calls the revelation healing and mercy for believers, and loss for wrongdoers.
Describes it as guidance and healing for some and as deafness for others.
Names the remembrance of God as what settles hearts, describing the same effect.

studies.applyIt: Pick one passage you find difficult, and instead of asking what it teaches, ask what it disturbs. Sit with the discomfort for a minute rather than resolving it. The verse puts healing before guidance, and treatment usually feels worse than instruction before it starts feeling better.
studies.explainEasier: God has sent people advice from their Lord. It heals what is wrong inside them, and it guides those who believe. Be glad about what God gives. That is worth more than anything you can save up.

studies.title: Who Gave You Permission
studies.meaning: The question begins with a fact nobody disputed. What people live on was sent down for them. Then it asks about something they had added to it. Certain animals and crops had been set aside as untouchable, and others declared free. The passage asks on whose authority. Two possibilities are offered, and only two. Either permission was given, or something is being put in God's mouth that He did not say. Early scholars note that the argument concerns the source of the rule, not the content of any one practice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Pre-Islamic Arabia had an elaborate set of consecrations, with camels dedicated to deities and released from work, animals whose milk was reserved, and portions of harvest assigned to shrines. The Quran names several of these practices elsewhere and states plainly that God did not institute them. This ayah does not list them; it asks the prior question about who is entitled to make such rules at all.

keyTerms.note: Anything a creature is given to live on, always implying a giver. Its use here sets up the whole question, since what has been received from someone is not obviously yours to reclassify.
From the root for the ear, so permission is pictured as something heard from the one entitled to grant it. The question is therefore about a transmission, not about whether a rule seems sensible.

The verb for cutting and stitching material into a finished shape. Used of speech about God it names manufacture, and the surah has already applied the same word to the charge made against the Prophet.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herds in Arabia carried marks of dedication that everyone could read. A camel that had produced a certain number of young might have its ear slit and be turned loose. It was never ridden or slaughtered. The animal grazed freely for the rest of its life. These dedications cost real wealth, and that is part of the point. People were making themselves poorer under rules whose origin nobody could name.
studies.didYouKnow: In another surah the Quran names four of these pre-Islamic dedications by their Arabic terms. It says directly that God did not set up any of them. That is one of very few places where the text keeps the technical vocabulary. It is the vocabulary of Arabian religious custom. Here in this surah the practices go unnamed. Only the question of who gave leave is put.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places a particular kind of error in speaking for God without warrant. That is treated as more serious than the practices themselves. A wrong rule can be corrected. A false attribution reshapes the picture of who God is. The passage also implies that provision arrives already ordered. Adding limits to it is a claim about the giver, not an act of caution.

crossReferences.why: Names four such consecrations by their Arabic terms and states that God did not institute them.
Warns against tongues declaring things permitted or banned in order to invent lies about God.
Asks who set aside the finery God produced for His servants and the good things of livelihood.

studies.applyIt: Notice one rule you follow that you cannot trace. A thing your family always avoided, a practice you picked up and never examined. Find out where it comes from this week. Some will turn out to be well grounded and some will be habit wearing the clothes of principle, and knowing which is which is the whole exercise.
studies.explainEasier: God sends food and other good things down for people. Some people then called part of it banned and part of it allowed. They were asked who told them to do that.

studies.title: Most Of Them Give No Thanks
studies.meaning: A question is left hanging instead of answered. What do people who invent things about God expect on the Day of Resurrection? Nothing is described. Early scholars note that the silence is the point. The questioners have not thought that far. Then the ayah turns to bounty. God is generous toward people, and most give no thanks. Put the two halves together. Making up rules about God and failing to thank Him for what He gave are the same failure, seen twice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It follows right after a question about who allowed people to reclassify their own provision. The pairing is on purpose.
