The surah moves from what people added to what they were given. No occasion is reported. The audience had inherited a set of consecrations that cost them real wealth. That makes the charge of thanklessness specific rather than general.

keyTerms.note: The same word the surah used earlier for holding beliefs without warrant. Here it asks what such people suppose about the outcome, so their habit of guessing is turned toward their own future.
From a root meaning what is left over and above. Bounty in this word is not what was owed but the excess beyond it, which is exactly what gratitude is a response to.
The root also describes a beast growing visibly fat on little pasture, so thanks is pictured as a small input producing an obvious return. Gratitude in this word shows on the outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Generosity in Arabia was public and remembered. A man who slaughtered for guests in a lean year had poems recited about him afterwards. Failing to thank a benefactor was a social offence with a name. Debts of thanks were tracked as closely as debts of money. Against that background, thanklessness toward the source of a whole livelihood would have looked like a serious breach of ordinary decency.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact statement that God is bountiful toward people while most give no thanks appears four times in the Quran, in four different surahs. In one it follows a story of thousands who fled death and were brought back to life. In another it closes a description of night and day. The same sentence is attached to gifts of very different kinds each time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage links two things we do not usually put together: false claims about God and plain ingratitude. Both describe the giver wrongly. One adds rules He did not set. The other fails to notice what He actually gave. That makes gratitude a matter of accuracy, not mood. It is getting the account right. The unanswered question about the Day then leaves the reader to supply what the fabricators have not.

crossReferences.why: States the same sentence about bounty and thanklessness in almost identical words.
Attaches the same statement to the gift of night for rest and day for seeing.
Says the favours of God cannot be counted, and names the human being as deeply unjust and thankless.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things you received this week that you did not arrange. Not blessings in a general sense: specific items, with names attached where a person was involved. Then thank one of those people directly today. Gratitude that stays inside the head is the exact thing this ayah is describing as absent.
studies.explainEasier: Some people make up rules and say they come from God. The verse asks what they think will happen on the last day. It also says God gives people a great deal, but most never say thank you.

studies.title: Not The Weight Of An Atom
studies.meaning: Three activities are named, then covered by one clause: any situation you are in, any part of the recitation you read, any work you do. The watching happens while you are caught up in the thing, not afterwards. Then the scale widens past human action. It reaches the smallest particle anyone in that world could name, and past it in both directions, smaller and larger. All of it is placed in a clear record. That turns watching into something kept.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It speaks first to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), then, mid-sentence, to everyone. The grammar shifts from singular to plural as it moves from reciting to doing. The reader is drawn in without being announced. The surah has argued about what God knows since its opening pages. Here the claim is stated at full extent rather than inside a dispute.

keyTerms.gloss: a matter, a state of affairs
keyTerms.note: Any business or condition a person is occupied with, however small. Its vagueness is deliberate, since a precise word would leave a gap and this clause is designed to leave none.
From a root for a liquid overflowing its container. It describes being absorbed and carried along by an activity, which is exactly the state in which people forget they can be seen.
The smallest thing that could be pointed at, read by the early scholars as a dust speck in a sunbeam or the smallest ant. It marks the limit of what people can tell apart, not of what exists.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sunlight through a gap in a tent roof makes dust visible in a way it never is otherwise. The classical scholars reach for exactly that image when they explain this word. Everyone had seen it. The point of the comparison was that these specks are real, countless and entirely beneath notice. That made them the best available name for something too small to matter.
studies.didYouKnow: Another surah pairs the same particle with the same clear record. It adds that nothing smaller or larger escapes His knowledge. It does so right after one of the three oaths the Prophet is told to swear. A further passage puts it differently. Not a leaf falls without His knowing, and no grain lies unknown in the darkness of the earth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being known is a present condition, not a future audit. The watching happens during the act. That changes its character: nothing is gathered later that is not already seen now. Pushing the claim below what people can perceive also removes a familiar category, the things too small to count. What follows is not mainly fear. It is a kind of company, since nothing a person does happens unseen.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same particle with a clear record, adding that nothing smaller or larger escapes Him.
States the same reach differently, no leaf falling and no grain in the darkness unrecorded.
Applies the claim to private conversations, with God present among any number who confer secretly.

studies.applyIt: Pick a small task today that nobody will inspect: how you park, how you fold something, how you answer a message you could ignore. Do it as though the standard were the same as for work that will be seen. The ayah is not asking for anxiety. It is asking whether your care depends on an audience.
studies.explainEasier: God sees everything you do while you are doing it, even the small things. Nothing is too tiny for Him to notice, on earth or in the sky. All of it is written down in a clear book.

studies.title: The Friends Of God
studies.meaning: An attention marker opens the passage, the particle used to announce something. Then a claim about the allies of God, followed by a definition that is deliberately plain: those who believed and used to guard themselves. No rank, no title, no separate class. Good news is promised in this life as well as the next, and the words are said to be unalterable. The last verse turns to the messenger and tells him not to be saddened by talk.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah aimed at people who claimed go-betweens and special access. Early scholars read the wording here as an answer to that. Who counts as a friend of God is fixed by two plain qualities, open to anybody. Classical sources record several readings of the good news promised in this life, including true dreams. They keep the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for nearness and for taking charge of someone. The word describes a two-sided closeness, which is why the same term is used of God towards believers elsewhere in the Quran.
From a root for skin and for the face brightening at news. The word names the physical effect of good news, so what is promised includes something felt rather than only something learned.
Strength that cannot be reached or reduced, the quality that made a fortified place impregnable. Saying that all of it belongs to God removes the standing the speakers were relying on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Holy men in Arabia held a recognised social role. Diviners, keepers of shrines and men credited with contact with the unseen were consulted and paid. They were treated as a class apart. A definition of God's friends that named only belief and self-restraint had no rite, lineage or shrine attached. It cut across an established trade and the fees that came with it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase promising no fear and no grief recurs through the Quran, always in the same shape. Here it is attached not to a named community but to a category defined in the verse that follows. Classical scholars treat the two verses as a single sentence for that reason. The claim would otherwise be left without a subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Closeness to God is described as available rather than handed out. The definition given is short enough to check yourself against. The good news promised in this life keeps the passage from being wholly postponed, without saying what it consists of. Early scholars leave that open. The instruction at the end then reframes opposition. What people say is answered by a statement about where power sits.

crossReferences.why: Names God as the ally of those who believe, the other side of the word used here.
Describes angels descending on those who stayed upright with the same reassurance.
States that all honour belongs to God, answering those who seek it elsewhere.

studies.applyIt: Check yourself against the definition rather than against an ideal. Two things are named, believing and guarding yourself. Neither requires a title. If the phrase friends of God has always sounded to you like a description of somebody else, notice that the passage spends its next line making sure it is not.
studies.explainEasier: The friends of God have nothing to fear and nothing to be sad about. They are simply the people who believe and are careful about how they live. Good news is waiting for them here and later.

studies.title: They Follow Only A Guess
studies.meaning: Ownership is announced first, and it is ownership of persons rather than things. Everyone in the heavens and everyone on earth belongs to God. That framing puts the partners of the next clause on the same list. Then comes a sharp claim, which early scholars unpack with care. Those who call on others are not really following partners at all, since there are none to follow. What they follow is their own supposition. The last word calls it guesswork.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has argued from several angles about speaking up for someone before God. It asked whether God could be unaware of such an office, and whether any partner could create or guide. This ayah takes the final step. It denies that the objects have any reality in the role assigned to them. The practice of the audience was inherited rather than argued for, which is what the closing charge names.

keyTerms.note: The relative pronoun used for beings with awareness rather than for objects. Choosing it here means the ownership announced covers persons, which quietly places the invoked partners among the owned.
The verb for judging fruit still on the tree before it is picked, a working practice in date farming. It names an educated guess, which makes it a mild word turned severe by its object.
From the vocabulary of shared ownership in a venture. Here it appears without the possessive ending used earlier in the surah, so the term is being examined in itself rather than as their claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Estimating a date harvest was a known skill. A man walked the grove before picking and judged what the trees would yield. The figure was used to settle shares and dues. Everyone accepted such estimates for practical use, and everyone knew they were only close. Borrowing that word for the base of a people's religion was a precise insult, and a quiet one.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb this ayah ends with, for judging unpicked fruit, appears only a handful of times in the Quran. Almost every time it describes guessing about God or the unseen. In one passage it closes a rebuke to people who claimed God willed their idol worship. They are first asked to produce any knowledge they have. The farming sense never appears on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that misdirected worship has no object at all. That is stronger than saying it has the wrong one. If the partners do not exist in the role given them, then what is followed is the worshipper's own construction. The practice turns back on itself. Announcing God's ownership of all persons first also removes the ground for the whole arrangement. Nothing that is owned can stand outside it as a go-between.

crossReferences.why: Calls the deities mere names devised by people and their forefathers, with no authority sent down.
Earlier in this surah, asks whether they are informing God of something He does not know.
Demands any knowledge they can produce, and says they follow nothing but conjecture.

studies.applyIt: Take one strong opinion you hold about how the unseen works. What happens after death, why a particular thing happened to you, what God thinks of someone. Ask where you got it. Some of it will be from the Book and some will be inherited atmosphere, and separating the two is the work this ayah is asking for.
studies.explainEasier: Everyone in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. People who pray to anything else are not really following those things at all. They are following their own ideas about them. They are only guessing.

studies.title: Night Made For Rest
studies.meaning: Two gifts are named, with two different kinds of purpose. The night is for settling. The word is about stillness and dwelling, not sleep alone. The day is described by what it does rather than what it is for: it is made to reveal. Early scholars note the difference. One is given a human purpose, the other a property. The closing clause then ties the signs to people who listen, a different group from the ones the surah named earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage moves between arguments about worship and reminders of what is already given. The surah opened with the sun and moon set for counting time. It comes back here to the same pair of intervals from a different angle. Now they are rest and sight rather than tools for counting. No occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.gloss: that you may settle, be still
keyTerms.note: From the root behind dwelling, stillness and a place of residence. It covers more than sleeping, naming the whole slackening of activity, which is why night is a home in this word rather than an interval.

An active form, so the day is described as doing the seeing rather than being seen in. The idiom credits the daylight with the vision it makes possible, which is closer to the experience than the literal sense.
The plain verb for hearing, used here for the group that benefits. The surah has already described people who listen without receiving anything, so the word carries a demand that goes past the ears.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in a settlement without lamplight was truly a stop. Work ended, animals were penned, and families gathered in one room around whatever fire there was. Nothing else could be done. Travellers did move at night to avoid the heat. For everyone else the dark ended the day's business outright. Rest was not one choice among many. It was what the dark left available.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran presses this pairing hardest in one passage. It asks the reader to imagine either interval made permanent. If the night ran on until the Day of Resurrection, it asks which god would bring light. If the day ran on, it asks which would bring night for rest. The gift is made visible there by taking it away, one half at a time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A gift nobody notices is put forward as evidence. The argument rests on the fact that the change from night to day never fails. That is exactly why it goes unremarked. The passage treats that invisibility as the problem, not as a weakness in the case. Naming those who listen as the ones who gain also implies that signs work through attention. What is offered is not new information. It is a different relation to what is already there.

crossReferences.why: Asks what would happen if either night or day were made permanent, and calls the pair a mercy.
States the same two purposes, rest and visibility, and calls them signs for people who believe.
Repeats the pairing and closes on bounty toward people who mostly give no thanks for it.

studies.applyIt: Notice tonight when you stop, and whether anything actually stops. Most of us now carry the working day into the dark on a screen. Try ending one activity an hour before sleep and doing nothing productive with that hour. The ayah calls the night a place to settle, and it is worth finding out whether yours still is one.
studies.explainEasier: God made the night so that people can stop and be still. He made the daylight so that they can see. Both of them come back every single day. The verse says there are signs in that for anyone who will listen.

studies.title: Saying What You Do Not Know
studies.meaning: A claim is quoted and answered in four moves. God is declared free of it. Then He is called the One who needs nothing. Then He is shown to own everything in the heavens and the earth. Early scholars note the order. Offspring answer a need: for help, for a line that continues, or for company. Each of those needs is closed off before the argument turns. Only then comes the demand for evidence. The ayah names the real offence as speaking about God without knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Several Arabian tribes called the angels daughters of God. The Quran answers that belief directly in other surahs. It sometimes notes the contradiction that the same people preferred sons for themselves. Claims about divine offspring were also known from other communities along the trade routes. This passage answers the general form of the claim, not any single version of it.

keyTerms.note: From the root for wealth and for being free of want. Placed here it does the argument's work directly, since offspring answer a lack, and the name denies that any lack exists.
The word for both political power and the evidence that authorises a claim. Its double sense is exact here: what is demanded is not persuasion but the standing to make the statement at all.
The general term covering son or daughter and any descendant. Its neutrality matters, since the reply does not correct the sex attributed but rules out the whole category of divine parenthood.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sons were security in Arabia. They fought for the clan, inherited the herds, and carried the name forward. A man without them was pitied, and daughters were sometimes treated as a burden. Children were the closest thing the culture had to insurance. To say that God needs nothing was to remove the strongest reason anyone in that society had for wanting them.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran answers this claim in surahs of very different lengths and tones. One passage says the heavens almost rupture and the mountains crumble at the words. Another replies that those called offspring are honoured servants. The shortest reply is four lines long and settles it by denying both directions at once, that He neither begets nor was begotten.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reasoning turns on sufficiency, not on dignity. To give God a child is to assume a need. The passage closes that assumption before it answers the claim. That is why the reply reads as calm rather than angry. Naming the offence as speaking without knowledge also widens it past this one error. The problem is a habit of making confident statements about God. This claim is only its most striking product.

crossReferences.why: Settles the same question in four lines, denying that He begets or was begotten.
Answers the claim by identifying those called offspring as honoured servants instead.
Asks how He could have a child when He never had a companion, and created all things.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you say what God wants, thinks or intends in a particular case. Sometimes you will be on solid ground. Sometimes you will be extending a general truth into a specific claim nobody gave you. Notice which one you are doing before the sentence leaves your mouth, and be willing to stop halfway.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said that God has a son. The verse answers that God needs nothing and already owns everything in the sky and on the earth. Then it asks them for proof, because they are saying things they do not know.

studies.title: Some Enjoyment, Then Return
studies.meaning: Three clauses run in sequence with nothing between them, and the compression is the point. A portion of enjoyment in this world, then the return, then the tasting of what follows. Early scholars note that the first item is not denied. Those who invent things about God do get something, and the ayah concedes it plainly rather than pretending the account is empty. What it disputes is the length of the entry and where the column ends.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes the argument that began with the claim that God has taken a child. The surah has just said that those who invent lies about God will not succeed. This ayah answers the obvious objection: they appear to be doing perfectly well. It sits immediately before the surah turns to Noah, whose people also appeared to be doing well.

keyTerms.note: Goods a traveller packs, useful precisely because they are temporary. The word grants the enjoyment its full reality while classifying it, since nobody confuses what is in the saddlebag with the destination.
A noun of place from the verb for returning, so it names the destination rather than the act. It implies the direction was always homeward, whatever the traveller thought he was doing.
The same verb the surah used earlier for a taste of mercy given after adversity. Repeating it here sets the two experiences in one vocabulary, so the contrast is in the object rather than the verb.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers packed for the road, not for the year. Dates, dried meat, water in skins, and enough for the stages between wells, all of it calculated to run out roughly when the journey ended. Nobody built a life around what was in the saddlebag. That everyday distinction between supplies and destination is exactly the one this ayah's central word carries.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for temporary provision runs through this surah as a quiet thread. It appeared earlier for what aggression buys, described as the enjoyment of the present life. Its root returns as a verb at the end of the Jonah account, for the comfort given to a people who believed. One root covers what is gained wrongly and what is granted mercifully.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses the two easy positions. It does not claim that wrongdoing fails to pay, which anyone can see is untrue. It does not treat the payment as final either. Instead it accepts the visible evidence and adds the part not yet visible. That leaves the reader without the comfort of thinking the unjust are secretly miserable. It leaves a harder question about time frames.

crossReferences.why: Warns against being impressed by the movements of the deniers, calling it brief enjoyment.
Uses the same structure, a little enjoyment before being driven to a harsh punishment.
Earlier in this surah, prices the gain of aggression with the identical word for provision.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person whose success bothers you because you think it is undeserved. Try dropping the private theory that they must be unhappy underneath. They may not be. Let the discomfort stand without resolving it, since the ayah does exactly that, and see whether your own choices still hold up without that consolation.
studies.explainEasier: People who make up lies about God may do well for a while. The verse says that is all they get: a little enjoyment now. Then they go back to God, and what comes next is not good at all.

studies.title: Decide, And Give Me No Respite
studies.meaning: Noah does not plead. He admits that his presence and his reminders have become unbearable to them. He states where his reliance rests. Then he invites his opponents to settle the matter. Gather everyone you can, make your decision clearly, and carry it out against me without delay. Early scholars note the third instruction, that their plan should not be obscure to them, as a demand for openness rather than plotting. What is offered is not defiance. It is a man declining to make himself easier to tolerate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah turns to earlier messengers at the point where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is facing organised hostility in a city he cannot leave. Noah's situation is drawn to match: a long mission, a community that will not hear, and a speaker who cannot withdraw. The Quran tells this story in several surahs and each version emphasises a different part of it.

keyTerms.gloss: my standing, my staying among you
keyTerms.note: A noun of place and time from the verb to stand. It covers his position, his continued presence and his standing up to speak, so what they find unbearable is his simply remaining there.
From a root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. Reliance in this word is a transfer of responsibility to someone competent, not a mood, which is why it is stated before the challenge.
From a root for covering over, used of clouds hiding the moon and of grief that clouds the heart. Telling them not to leave their plan obscure asks for it in the open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public arbitration required both sides to state their case plainly. A grievance kept unspoken was treated as a danger to everyone. When a clan meant to act against a man it would usually declare it. A withdrawal of protection announced in the open worked better than a private one. The demand of Noah that their decision be clear and unhidden would have sounded like a call to proper procedure.
studies.didYouKnow: Noah's story is told across many surahs, and the versions differ in what they preserve. One gives his complaint that people thrust fingers in their ears and wrapped themselves in their garments. Another records the notables dismissing his followers as the lowest among them. This surah keeps almost none of the narrative and preserves only the challenge, which appears nowhere else in these words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is shown to produce boldness rather than passivity. Noah invites the worst his opponents can do, precisely because he has placed the outcome elsewhere. That reverses the usual assumption that trust means waiting quietly. The passage also declines to make his position sympathetic. He does not ask them to understand him, and he does not soften what he is doing to them. That is a rarer kind of honesty than defiance.

crossReferences.why: Gives the opening of the same mission and the notables' reply dismissing his followers.
Preserves Noah's own account of calling night and day, openly and then privately.
Earlier in this surah, the Prophet faces the same demand to make himself easier to accept.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you have softened lately so that people around you would find you easier. Sometimes that is kindness and sometimes it is retreat. You usually know which. Pick one case and state it plainly again this week, without heat and without apology. Notice what the softening had been costing you.
studies.explainEasier: Noah told his people that if they could not stand having him around, they should make up their minds. He said they could plan together and then do whatever they wanted to him. He had put his trust in God.

studies.title: I Asked You For Nothing
studies.meaning: Noah answers the chance of rejection by taking his own stake out of the argument. He has asked for no payment, so turning away costs him nothing that was ever on the table. What he does receive falls due from God alone. Then he names his own position. He says he was commanded to be among those who submit, which puts him under the same instruction he has been delivering. Early scholars note that this is the standard reply of messengers across the Quran, repeated almost word for word by several of them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Religious functionaries in Arabia were maintained by offerings, and custodians of shrines drew income from pilgrims, so an unpaid preacher was an unfamiliar figure. The question of what the messenger stood to gain was a live one in Mecca, where opponents had reportedly offered wealth and position to end the matter. Noah's words answer that suspicion from a great distance.

keyTerms.note: Payment for work done, the ordinary commercial term for hire. Its use twice in one sentence sets the transaction up and then relocates it, so the same word covers what is refused and what is expected.
Passive, so the speaker appears as one under orders rather than as the one giving them. It puts the messenger inside the message, subject to the same authority as the people he is addressing.
From a root meaning to hand something over whole and to be at peace. The Quran applies it to prophets long before the seventh century, describing a posture rather than a later community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poets, soothsayers and shrine keepers all lived off their audiences. A poet praised a patron and was rewarded. A diviner took a fee for consulting the arrows. The keepers of a sanctuary drew on what pilgrims brought. Speech in that economy had a price. A man who spoke in public for years without collecting was doing something the culture had no ready name for.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who submit appears twice in this surah. The two uses could hardly be further apart in circumstance. Noah uses it here for the standing he was commanded to take. Pharaoh uses it of himself much later in the surah, with the sea already closing over him. The answer he receives is that the moment has passed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Refusing payment is part of the message, not personal virtue. A messenger with no fee has no reason to bend his content to his audience. The disclaimer protects what is being said. Placing himself among those who submit does something further. It denies him any exemption. Whatever he asks of them is already binding on him. That removes the last suspicion that the arrangement pays the speaker.

crossReferences.why: Has Noah say the same thing in a different surah, no payment asked, his reward with the Lord.
Adds his refusal to dismiss the poorer believers whom the notables wanted removed.
States the principle as advice, to follow those who ask no wage and are themselves guided.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you do for others and ask honestly what you are collecting for it. Money is the easy case; usually it is gratitude, standing, or being needed. Try doing that same thing once this week in a way that pays you none of it, and notice how much harder it becomes.
studies.explainEasier: Noah told his people that he had never asked them for money. If they walked away, he lost nothing. God would pay him instead. He said he had been told to be one of the people who give themselves to God.

studies.title: Made Them The Successors
studies.meaning: A long mission is compressed into one line of consequence. They called him a liar. The small group in the vessel was brought through. Those who rejected the signs went under. The middle detail is the one that carries. The survivors were made successors, so the earth was not left empty but handed over. Early scholars note the closing instruction. It is addressed to the present audience rather than to the people of Noah, telling them to look at how it ended for those who had been warned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It is told to a small, pressed community whose situation the story matches at every point except the ending. The Quran gives the account of Noah in several surahs with different details kept. Some describe the building of the vessel, others the son who refused to board. This surah keeps only the outcome, which is what its argument needs at this stage.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb for rescuing, used of pulling someone clear of something already closing in. It names extraction from danger rather than the danger being removed, which fits a flood exactly.
The general word for a vessel, the same one this surah used earlier for merchant ships caught in a storm. Nothing in the term marks it as extraordinary; it is simply the thing that floats.
Plural of the one who comes after and takes another's place. It carries no honour by itself, only the fact of standing on ground that has just been vacated by someone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Flash floods were the peninsula's most familiar catastrophe. A dry valley could fill within an hour from rain nobody had seen fall, and whole camps were carried off by water that arrived without warning and drained away by morning. Everyone knew the sound of it coming down a wadi. Drowning was not an exotic death in that landscape; it was the one that came out of a clear sky.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the survivors becoming successors occurs four times in the Quran. Two of them are in this surah. The earlier one speaks to the audience directly. It tells them they were made successors on earth after the generations before them, so that God might see how they behave. The same term links the survivors of Noah to the people being warned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is described as continuation rather than escape. The people brought through do not simply survive. They inherit. The story does not end with rescue but with new occupants on the same terms as the last. That connects to the earlier statement in this surah about succession as a test. The closing instruction to look at the outcome also treats history as evidence, open to anyone willing to examine it.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same events in almost identical words, the denial, the rescue, and the drowning.
Uses the same word for successors of the audience itself, made to occupy ground others vacated.
Preserves the instructions for building and loading the vessel, which this surah omits entirely.

studies.applyIt: Find out one thing about the people who held your position before you: at work, in a family role, in a group you joined. Almost nobody asks. Learn what they did well and where they came unstuck. That is the closest version of what this ayah asks, which is simply to look at how it went.
studies.explainEasier: The people of Noah called him a liar. God saved him and those with him in the ship, and let them live on after the others. The people who turned down the signs drowned. The verse says to look at how that ended.

studies.title: A Seal On The Hearts
studies.meaning: The pattern after Noah is described as a repetition, not a series of new events. Messengers came with clear proofs. They met people who would not believe in what they had already rejected before the proofs arrived. Early scholars read the sealing that follows as the settled result of that order. It is not an obstacle placed in the way beforehand. The refusal comes first in the sentence and the seal comes second, which is how the classical sources handle the grammar.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is moving through earlier peoples on its way to Moses. This ayah covers the whole stretch between them in one line. Nearly identical wording appears in another surah as the summary of several ruined towns. The audience being addressed had themselves rejected the message before looking at it. The surah said so plainly some thirty verses earlier.

keyTerms.note: From a root for something plainly separated and evident. Using it here concedes that the evidence was adequate, which is what makes the refusal a fact about the audience rather than about the case.
The verb for pressing a die into clay or metal, the action that closes a document or mints a coin. A seal fixes a shape and marks a thing as finished, which is the force it carries here.
From a root for going past a limit, used of aggression and of exceeding a set measure. It names the ones sealed by their conduct, so the description is earned rather than assigned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seals were how a document became final. A merchant's mark pressed into wax or clay closed a letter and vouched for it, and breaking a seal was a serious act with witnesses. Sealed containers of goods travelled the trade routes unopened between ports. The image is not of something locked away for safekeeping but of a matter formally concluded, with nothing further to be added.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this sealing image in several places, and always states a cause alongside it. One passage attaches it to those who do not know. Another attaches it to every arrogant tyrant. A third gives the same sequence found here: proofs came, they would not believe what they had already rejected, and then the sealing. The order of the clauses stays the same throughout.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a hardening that follows conduct rather than coming before it. That is how the classical scholars read the sequence. It keeps both the reality of the outcome and the responsibility of the person. What closes is closed by a pattern the person set. It also implies something about repetition. Each refusal makes the next one easier, until the position is no longer chosen but simply occupied.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sequence in nearly identical words, as the summary of several destroyed towns.
Attaches the same sealing to those who do not know, stated as a general practice.
Applies it to those who argue against the signs without proof, naming the arrogant bully.

studies.applyIt: Notice a small thing you have said no to so often that you no longer consider it: an invitation, a form of exercise, a way of praying. Say yes once this week, purely to check whether the refusal is still a decision. Most of them turn out to be grooves rather than judgements. The only way to find out is to try one.
studies.explainEasier: After Noah, God kept sending messengers with clear proof. Each time, people had already made up their minds and would not believe. So their hearts were sealed shut. The verse says this is what happens to people who keep going too far.

studies.title: Sent To Pharaoh And His Court
studies.meaning: One sentence sets up the longest story in the surah. Two brothers are sent together. The signs come from God rather than from them. Those who receive them are named as a ruler and the notables around him. Early scholars note the pairing of the audience. It is not a people but a court, since in Egypt the decision belonged to a small circle. The response is given as arrogance before it is given as denial, which puts the obstacle in their standing rather than in the evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran returns to Moses more often than to any other prophet, and this surah's version is comparatively short, focused on the contest with the sorcerers and the crossing. Its audience faced their own council of notables, a small group of families whose agreement decided what Mecca did. The parallel is not stated but the shape of the story matches it closely.

keyTerms.note: The same word used for verses of scripture and for features of the natural world. Attaching it to what Moses carried keeps miracle and revelation inside one category, both being things that point rather than compel.
From a root meaning to fill, so the word names those who fill a council chamber or an eye with their presence. It denotes the men whose agreement a ruler needs, not the population.
A form of the verb for greatness that adds seeking it for oneself. The response is described as a claim about their own standing rather than as a judgement about the evidence in front of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was run by an assembly of leading men from the main clans. No serious matter went ahead without them. A newcomer with a claim did not address the city. He addressed that circle, and its verdict then held for everyone. The audience hearing this ayah knew exactly what a court of notables was. They knew how much a message depended on whether such men felt their position threatened by it.
studies.didYouKnow: Moses is named more times in the Quran than any other prophet. His story is told across dozens of surahs, with different portions kept in each. Another surah records his own hesitation before this mission. It gives his fear of being rejected and his request that his brother be sent with him. The reply was that they should go together, because God would be listening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sending two rather than one matters quietly. It makes the mission a shared burden and gives it a witness. Naming the addressees as a ruler and his circle also places the resistance precisely, in the people with most to lose. The word for their response then makes arrogance the first obstacle to belief in this account. That is a claim about character rather than about argument, and the surah builds on it from here.

crossReferences.why: Gives the sending of the two brothers, with the instruction to speak to Pharaoh gently.
Preserves Moses' hesitation and his request that Aaron be sent alongside him.
Opens the same episode with nearly identical wording and the same closing instruction to consider the end.

studies.applyIt: Think of an idea you rejected recently. Ask whether any part of the refusal was about your position rather than the idea. Would accepting it have meant admitting in public that you were wrong, or losing standing with someone. Name that honestly once. The passage points to this obstacle before it points to any argument.
studies.explainEasier: God sent Moses and his brother Aaron to the king of Egypt and the powerful men around him. They brought clear signs from God. But those men were too proud to listen. They were people who did wrong.

studies.title: Do You Call Truth Sorcery
studies.meaning: A verdict is delivered before anything is examined, and Moses answers by putting their own sentence back to them as a question. Is this what you say about truth when it reaches you. Then a second question that refuses to argue on their terms, asking whether this is sorcery at all, followed by a flat statement that those who practise it do not come through. Early scholars note that Moses does not defend the sign. He examines the speech used about it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge of sorcery had already been made in the second verse of this surah, against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). An audience reaching this passage meets the same word twice: once about themselves and once about Egypt. Sorcery was a recognised trade in the ancient world, with practitioners attached to courts. That is why the accusation was plausible rather than merely abusive.

keyTerms.note: The emphatic particle attached to the noun makes the verdict absolute. What was in fact a guess about an unfamiliar event is delivered in the grammar of certainty, which is the feature Moses picks up on.
A question about their speech rather than about their belief. It treats a spoken verdict as an act with consequences, separate from whatever the speakers privately think about the matter.
The root belongs to the farmer splitting open the ground, so success means breaking through to something buried. The same verb was used earlier in this surah of those who fabricate about God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Words carried legal weight in Arabia in a way that is hard to picture now. A public declaration could bind a clan, end a marriage or withdraw protection. There was no writing to soften the effect. Everyone understood that saying a thing aloud in front of others was doing something, not reporting an opinion. Moses questions the saying, because in that world the saying was the act.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for prospering that closes this passage appears twice in this surah, each time with the same negative. It is used near the beginning of those who make up lies about God. It is used again here of sorcerers. Another surah puts the same denial in the mouth of Moses at the contest itself: the magician does not succeed, whatever he does.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a hasty verdict as a moral act, not a slip of thinking. What people say about truth when it arrives is shown to reveal something about them. That is why Moses answers the sentence instead of the objection behind it. There is also a quiet claim in the second question. Sorcery and revelation can be told apart, and anyone willing to look before speaking can do it.

crossReferences.why: Has Moses state the same principle at the contest, that the magician does not succeed anywhere.
Records the identical verdict in almost the same words when the clear signs reached them.
Opens this surah with the same accusation of sorcery, made against a different messenger.

studies.applyIt: Catch one verdict you deliver aloud today with more certainty than you actually have. About a person's motives, a news story, a decision at work. Notice the gap between what you know and how you said it. You do not have to correct it publicly; simply hearing the gap once is what this passage is asking for.
studies.explainEasier: When the truth reached them from God, they called it plain magic. Moses asked them how they could say that about truth as soon as it arrived. He told them that people who do magic never win in the end.

studies.title: So That Greatness Becomes Yours
studies.meaning: Two objections are raised together and neither concerns whether the message is true. The first is inheritance: you would turn us from what our fathers were found upon. The second is suspicion of motive: you two want the standing in this land for yourselves. Early scholars note that the second charge is a projection, since the men making it held exactly that standing. The reply is not spoken. Pharaoh simply calls for every skilled sorcerer, and Moses tells them to throw first.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Appeals to ancestral practice were the standard reply to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in Mecca. The Quran records them in several surahs in almost these words. Charges that he sought leadership were also current, and reports describe offers of kingship made to buy off the message. This episode from Egypt therefore carries a double reading for its first audience.

keyTerms.note: From a root for twisting the head to look aside. The image is of being pulled off a line of sight rather than argued out of a position, which is how inherited custom is usually defended.

An intensive noun for absolute pre-eminence, used elsewhere in the Quran only of God's own greatness in the heavens and the earth. Applying it to a human position is what makes the accusation revealing.
A plain imperative with no challenge in it. Moses lets them go first and lets them finish, which places the whole demonstration after theirs rather than in competition with it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ancestral practice was the strongest argument available in Arabia. Lineage was memorised. Custom was inherited along with the herds. A man kept his standing by being known as the son of his father. Leaving what the forefathers did was not a private choice. It read as a claim that they had been wrong, which touched every living relative. That is why the objection here comes first and the question of truth never arrives.
studies.didYouKnow: The word these objectors use for the greatness they suspect Moses of wanting appears only twice in the Quran. The other time, it declares that such greatness in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone. The court of Pharaoh reaches for the largest word available and applies it to a position in Egypt. Then it accuses two brothers of wanting what those men already held.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ways of dodging a claim sit side by side, and neither one meets it. Appealing to inheritance answers a question about truth with a question about loyalty. Doubting the motives of the messenger makes the argument needless by staining the arguer. Both moves are as easy now as they were then. The passage also lets the contest go ahead on the terms of the opponents. That suggests truth does not need the first move.

crossReferences.why: Records the same appeal to ancestors and notes it was made by the wealthy in every town.
Gives the objection plainly, following what the forefathers followed even if they understood nothing.
States that the greatness these men suspect Moses of wanting belongs to God in heaven and earth.

studies.applyIt: Take one practice you keep because it is what your family does, and separate two questions. Is it good, and is it yours. Both answers can be yes, and often are. The failure the passage describes is not honouring your parents but letting inheritance stand in for the first question entirely.
studies.explainEasier: The men around the king told Moses he only wanted to pull them away from what their fathers did, and to grab power for himself. They said they would never believe him. Then the king sent for every skilled magician.

studies.title: God Does Not Prosper Corruption
studies.meaning: Moses names what has been thrown, then makes two statements in the future tense. God will bring it to nothing. God does not set right the work of those who spread ruin. Early scholars note that the second is a general principle, not a comment on the events of that day. What is claimed is a pattern in how things go, not a single act. The closing line adds the positive half. Truth is made to stand by the words of God, and the dislike of the guilty does not enter into it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the turning point of the contest. Other surahs keep the detail that the sorcerers were promised reward and a place near the throne if they won. They also record that some of them believed once they saw the outcome. This surah keeps only the statement of Moses. It leaves out both the reward and the aftermath, which holds the focus on the principle rather than the spectacle.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what is void and without substance. The prefix marks near future, so the claim is not that the work was never impressive but that it is about to be shown to have nothing in it.
The verb for repairing and making sound, the direct opposite of the word used for those who spread ruin. God is described as declining to mend what such work produces, which leaves it to fall apart.
Verb and object from one root, an emphatic construction the translation cannot carry. Truth is not merely revealed but made to stand, which implies it needs establishing rather than only announcing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian audiences knew practised illusion. Diviners, snake handlers and men who read the future from arrows or bird flight worked the markets and the fairs, and part of the entertainment lay in not knowing how it was done. Nobody in that culture doubted such skills existed. What this passage claims is not that the display was fake but that work of this kind does not hold up.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states the same outcome elsewhere in almost the same structure. It says God confirms the truth and voids falsehood, even though the guilty dislike it. Another passage puts it as an announcement: truth has come and falsehood has withered, since falsehood is bound to wither. The pairing of the two verbs, establishing and voiding, holds wherever it appears.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is claimed is a tendency built into how things run, not a rescue that arrives when needed. Work founded on ruin fails because nothing holds it up, not because it is struck down. That difference changes how a person waits. The last clause is just as deliberate. Truth is made to stand whether or not anyone welcomes it. That takes agreement off the list of things truth depends on.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of actions, confirming the truth and nullifying falsehood despite the guilty.
States the outcome as an announcement, truth arrived and falsehood bound to wither away.
Gives the sequel this surah omits, the sorcerers defeated and then believing.

studies.applyIt: Think of something built on a shortcut that you watched come apart later. A relationship begun dishonestly, a project whose numbers were arranged. Notice that it usually did not collapse all at once. It simply failed to hold. Then look at what you are building now, and ask which parts you are counting on nobody examining.
studies.explainEasier: The magicians threw down their tricks. Moses told them it was magic, and that God would make it come to nothing. God does not let the work of people who wreck things last. Truth is what God makes stand.

studies.title: Only A Few Young Ones
studies.meaning: After a public win, the result is counted honestly and it is small. Only some young people believed. They did so in fear of being broken by Pharaoh and his circle. Early scholars differ over whose young these were. Some read them as descendants of the Israelites, others as young people from among the people of Pharaoh, and the sources record both. The last two clauses explain the fear rather than the failure. The man was high in the land, and he went past every limit.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the parallel would have been plain. The early community in Mecca was small and mostly young. It included people with no clan to protect them, who suffered for it. The account here does not inflate the response to a miracle. It records that a demonstration everyone saw produced a handful of believers, all of them afraid.

keyTerms.note: From a root for scattering seed. It names descendants and, by extension, the young of a people. The word is indefinite here, so the number is left small and unspecified rather than counted.
The root describes ore heated in fire to separate the metal. It covers persecution and trial together, so the fear named is of being put through something that would show what they were made of.
From the root for height, used of the ruler's position rather than his character. The Quran elsewhere applies the same root to God, so the word quietly names what the man was claiming.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The young were the least protected and the most free. A man with a household, a trade and duties to a clan had everything to lose by taking an unpopular side. A young person had fewer ties and less standing to guard. The first Meccan community showed the same pattern clearly. It explains why a display that convinced everyone changed the minds only of those with least to defend.
studies.didYouKnow: Another surah preserves what the fear in this ayah points to. It records the chiefs urging Pharaoh to act against Moses and his people. His reply was that their sons would be killed and their women spared. A further passage has him say plainly that he means to kill Moses. The threat this ayah leaves unnamed is spelled out elsewhere in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records an outcome that is honest rather than cheering. A sign that settled the argument in public did not produce a movement. That separates the truth of a claim from how it is received, once again. It also treats fear as a real factor without excusing it or condemning it. Those who believed did so while afraid. The ayah states that as a fact about their belief, not as a mark against it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the threat behind the fear, the chiefs urging action and the answer about killing sons.
Records Pharaoh's intention to kill Moses and a believer in his own household hiding his faith.
Describes the same exaltation in the land, dividing the people and weakening one group among them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you hold quietly that would cost you something to say aloud in a particular room. You do not have to say it today. Just notice that the ayah counts people who believed while afraid as believers, and that it does not ask them to stop being afraid first.
studies.explainEasier: Even after all this, only a few young people believed in Moses. They were scared of what the king and his men would do to them. The king had huge power in the land, and he used it to go far past any limit.

studies.title: Do Not Make Us A Trial
studies.meaning: Moses puts reliance as a condition rather than a comfort: if you have believed, then rely on Him, if you have submitted. The reply comes back as a prayer in two parts. First, do not make us a trial for the oppressors, which the early scholars read either as asking not to be the means by which the oppressors are misled into thinking themselves right, or as asking not to be tested through them. Second, deliver us by Your mercy. The word for mercy is not decorative; deliverance is asked as a gift, not as a wage.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and a community under pressure in its own city would have recognised the prayer at once. Believers there had watched people suffer for their position while opponents prospered. The worry that this looked like a verdict was a real one. A prayer in another surah uses almost the same words. It asks not to be made a target for those who disbelieve.

keyTerms.note: From the root for appointing an agent to act for you. It names a transfer of responsibility to someone competent, which is why it can be commanded here rather than merely encouraged.
From ore heated to separate the metal. Asking not to be made one for the oppressors means either not being the instrument that hardens them or not being the material put through the fire.
The root belongs to the womb, so the word carries the protectiveness of a mother toward what she carries. Deliverance is asked on that basis rather than on the basis of anything they had done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A defeated party in Arabia lost more than the fight. Its gods were held to have failed, its claims were discredited, and the victors read the outcome as vindication. Everyone understood that events were treated as verdicts. That is exactly the danger in this prayer: not the suffering itself, but the conclusion their suffering would let the powerful draw about who was right.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrasing of this prayer comes back in the Quran with a different verb. It asks that the believers not be made a target for those who disbelieve. Two prophets in the Quran use the reliance verb at moments of open weakness. In both cases it follows a practical arrangement rather than replacing one. Reliance in these passages is what is done after the planning, never instead of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is offered as the test of a claim, not as comfort for the weak. Moses makes it conditional on belief itself. Refusing to rely would put the belief in question. The prayer that follows is unusual for what it leaves out. It does not ask for victory, and it does not ask for the oppressors to be destroyed. It asks that the believers not become the evidence by which wrongdoing proves itself. That is a concern about truth rather than about safety.

crossReferences.why: Prays in nearly the same words, asking not to be made a target for those who disbelieve.
Shows a prophet taking a practical precaution and then declaring reliance in the same breath.
Gives the reply of believers told that people had mobilised, that God is enough for them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a hard situation you are in and notice what you are actually asking for. Most of us ask for the outcome. Try adding one line asking that your conduct inside it not give anyone a reason to think badly of what you believe. That is the specific request this prayer makes, and it is rarely the first one that occurs to us.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told his people that if they really believed in God, they should trust Him. They said they did. Then they asked God not to let cruel people use them, and to save them by His mercy.

studies.title: Make Your Homes Places Of Worship
studies.meaning: Under persecution, the instruction is not to flee but to change the houses. Early scholars divide over the middle phrase. Some read it as setting the homes toward a common direction for prayer. Others read it as making the homes themselves the place of prayer, because gathering in the open was no longer safe. The classical sources record both without choosing. Either way, the arrangement is domestic. The passage closes by telling the two brothers to give the believers good news, which is what the whole instruction amounts to.
studies.historicalContext: The setting is Egypt, under a ruler just described as high in the land and past all limits. It is addressed to a community that could not worship in the open. The surah is Meccan. Its first audience included people who prayed quietly in houses on the edge of the city, because praying at the sanctuary drew abuse. The instruction reads differently to a community in that position.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking up residence and preparing a place to stay, addressed here to two people. Its choice makes the instruction one about staying put rather than about temporary shelter during a crisis.

From the root for facing and for what is in front. The commentators read it either as a common orientation for prayer or as making the houses themselves the place faced, and both readings are preserved.
From the root for skin, since news shows first in the face. The imperative turns singular here after two plurals, so the instruction to encourage is given to one man in particular.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Houses in the ancient Near East were crowded and used for everything, with animals, storage and sleeping set around one courtyard. Turning one into a place of worship meant no building work. It meant clearing a corner and agreeing what it was for. Early Muslims in Mecca did something similar. They prayed in the ravines outside the city and in private courtyards when the sanctuary became impossible.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where a home is given the word for a direction faced in prayer. The term appears elsewhere in the passage about the change of prayer direction in Medina. The classical scholars discuss this ayah at length just because the usage is unique. Another passage speaks instead of houses God has allowed to be raised, where His name is celebrated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is shown to survive the loss of its public setting. When a community cannot gather, the instruction is not to stop but to move the practice indoors. That implies the essential thing was never the building. Attaching good news to the same instruction is also pointed. A community reduced to praying at home is told this is not a defeat. The encouragement arrives as part of the arrangement rather than afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Speaks of houses God permitted to be raised where His name is celebrated morning and evening.
Gives Moses the same joining of recognising God with establishing prayer for His remembrance.
Uses the related idea of a place taken for prayer, at the House rather than in a home.

studies.applyIt: Choose one spot in your home and make it the place you pray, even if you usually pray anywhere. A corner, a particular direction, a mat that stays out. Give it a week. The instruction here is about a physical arrangement, and most people find that having a place changes how often they use it.
studies.explainEasier: God told Moses and his brother to settle their people in Egypt and to turn their own homes into places of prayer. They were to keep praying there. And they were to give the believers good news.

studies.title: Obliterate Their Wealth
studies.meaning: The prayer opens by naming what God Himself gave: splendour and wealth in the present life. Then it states what that is being used for, to lead people off the path. Only then comes the request, and it is severe. Blot out their wealth and harden their hearts. Early scholars read the second half as asking that the case against them be completed, not as asking for their ruin. They note that the prayer follows years of open rejection rather than one provocation.
studies.historicalContext: The setting is Egypt after the contest, with a court that has seen a public demonstration and dug in further. The surah is Meccan, addressed to people watching opponents prosper in plain sight. Prayers of this kind appear elsewhere in the Quran on the lips of prophets after long refusal. The classical sources treat them as coming at the end of a mission rather than during it.

keyTerms.note: Ornament that catches the eye, used in the Quran for the earth in bloom and for a person's display. Naming it as given by God prevents the prayer from treating their wealth as stolen.
The verb for wiping out a track in sand or a written mark until nothing can be read. It asks for erasure rather than transfer, so nobody gains what is taken away.
To fasten something firmly, as a load is lashed to a camel. Applied to hearts it asks that a position already taken be fixed in place, which the early scholars read as sealing a settled refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that world was display. A man's standing was read off his herds, the cloth he wore and how many he could feed, and there was no way to hold riches privately. Opponents of a message could therefore be seen prospering every day in the street. The prayer's first clause, acknowledging that the splendour came from God, is the difficult part for anyone watching that.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran preserves several prayers of this kind from prophets, and each one comes after the mission has been exhausted rather than in its early years. Noah's is the starkest, asking that no dweller be left on the earth, and it is stated together with his reason. In every case the text supplies the history first and the request second.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is careful in a way that is easy to miss. It grants that the wealth of opponents came from God. That refuses the comfortable thought that success proves wrongdoing. It then asks for something a person cannot bring about, which keeps the matter a request rather than a plan. A prayer this severe is left in the record without being made a model, since what comes before it is a lifetime of refusal.

crossReferences.why: Gives Noah's comparable prayer at the end of his mission, with the reason he offers for it.
Describes the pattern this prayer assumes, affluence transgressing until the word falls due.
Shows wealth given and then used against the people it came among, in the same generation.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk to God about someone who has wronged you. Most of us either censor the anger entirely or let it run. This prayer does neither: it states the facts first, including the inconvenient one that their good fortune also came from God. Try beginning there next time, and see what survives the honesty.
studies.explainEasier: Moses prayed about the king and his men. He said God had given them all their shine and money, and they were using it to pull people away from God. So he asked God to wipe that wealth out.

studies.title: Your Prayer Is Answered
studies.meaning: The answer arrives in three parts and only the first is what was asked for. The prayer has been responded to. Then two instructions follow: hold your course, and do not walk the road of those who do not know. Early scholars note the plural verbs, so both brothers are addressed even though one of them did the speaking. What is striking is the shape of the reply. Being answered comes with a warning attached, as though the danger begins after the request is granted.
studies.historicalContext: The setting is Egypt at the end of the dealings of Moses with the court. Classical sources record a long gap between this answer and its effect. Some give many years, and they treat the gap as part of the lesson. The surah is Meccan. It speaks to a community whose own prayers had been running for years with no visible result, which is the situation this exchange answers.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb in the completed tense, so the answering is already a fact at the moment of speaking. Nothing is said about when the effect will appear, and the grammar deliberately separates the two.
From the root for standing and for what is straight, in a form meaning to keep oneself so. It describes maintaining a line already set rather than finding one, which is why it follows the answer.
The description given to the road not to be followed. It names a lack of knowledge rather than hostility, which makes the warning about drifting into ignorance rather than about joining opponents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan that got good news at a waypoint still had the hardest stages ahead. Word could arrive that the route was clear, or that the price at the destination had risen. The response was not celebration but keeping formation for the remaining weeks. Everyone who travelled knew the danger often lies in the stretch after the worry lifts, when attention slackens.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to hold straight appears elsewhere in the Quran, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Once it comes with the added phrase, along with those who repented with you. Once it comes right after the statement that he is only a human like his listeners. In each place the command follows a moment of reassurance rather than a moment of difficulty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answered prayer is treated as a beginning, not a conclusion. The two instructions that follow imply that the risk after being granted something is drift. The pressure that kept a person upright has been removed. Naming the other road as one of ignorance rather than malice is also precise. Most people do not choose the wrong path. They stop paying attention, and the passage puts the warning exactly there.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same command to hold straight, extended to those who repented alongside him.
Places the same instruction directly after a statement of the messenger's ordinary humanity.
The prayer this ayah answers, offered immediately before in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Recall something you prayed for and received. Look at the period just after it arrived rather than the waiting. That is usually where things loosened: the routine that got you through, the attention you were paying. Pick one habit from your hardest season and put it back this week, while nothing is going wrong.
studies.explainEasier: God told Moses that his prayer had been heard. Then He gave two orders. Keep going straight, both of you. And do not take the road of people who do not know anything about God.

studies.title: Belief As The Water Closes
studies.meaning: The crossing is given in half a line. The pursuit gets two words describing its temper: aggression and hostility. Then the moment. With drowning already reaching him, the ruler declares belief. Early scholars note the wording. He does not name God directly but identifies Him as the one the Children of Israel believe in. They read this as the theology of a man who has just lost an argument rather than found something. He ends by placing himself among those who submit.
studies.historicalContext: The setting is the sea crossing, the last scene of the account of Moses in this surah. The story was known in outline across Arabia through contact with Jewish communities. The Quran tells it in several surahs, with different portions kept in each. This version keeps almost nothing of the crossing itself. It gives its full attention to what the pursuer said at the end.

keyTerms.note: The same root the surah used earlier for violations committed after being rescued at sea. The word returns here for a man doing exactly that, and the sea is again the setting.
The verb for catching something you have been chasing. Its use is exact and bitter, since the pursuer is finally overtaken himself, by the water rather than by anyone he was hunting.
From a root meaning to hand over whole and to be at peace. Earlier in this surah Noah says he was commanded to be among them; here the same word is claimed at the last possible instant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was a special dread for people who mostly could not swim. They feared the sea as a place with no footing and no bargaining. Arabian storytelling about the sea is full of that helplessness. A powerful man taken by water was the clearest image available of authority meeting something that cares nothing for rank. That is what makes this scene land as it does.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who submit occurs twice in this surah, at the two ends of its story section. Noah uses it for the standing he was commanded to take. Pharaoh uses it of himself with the sea already closing. The same claim is made by a man at the start of a long faithful life and by a man at the end of a hostile one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates recognition from repentance. Everything the man says is true, and its truth changes nothing. Belief that arrives only when the alternative is gone describes circumstances, not a turn of the heart. The grammar of the declaration says the same. He identifies God through the people he was pursuing, not in his own words. Facts were never what he lacked.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind this scene, that faith at the sight of the punishment does not avail.
Records the same request at the point of death, asking to be sent back, and its refusal.
The other occurrence of the same word in this surah, spoken by Noah about his own standing.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you will admit eventually because circumstances will force it. A doctor's finding, a truth about a relationship, a limit you have reached. Say it out loud today while you still could pretend otherwise. The whole distance in this ayah is between an admission you made and one that was made for you.
studies.explainEasier: God brought the Children of Israel safely across the sea. The king and his army chased after them. As the water was about to take him, the king said he believed in the God of Israel.

studies.title: A Sign For Those After
studies.meaning: The reply to the drowning man is one word and a summary of his record. Then something unexpected. What is preserved is not the man but the body, kept so that those who come after have a sign. Early scholars differ on the term used. Some read it as his corpse cast up on the shore. Others read it as his armour, since the word can carry that sense, and the sources record both. The ayah then closes on the general failure. Most people pay no attention to signs at all.
studies.historicalContext: The setting closes the account of Moses in this surah. The Quran does not name the ruler here or anywhere else. The classical scholars declined to fix a date or a dynasty. What the passage claims is that a sign was left behind for later generations. It then notes at once how little difference such things usually make.

keyTerms.note: The word normally means the trunk of a body, and the early Arabic dictionary writers also record a sense of a coat of mail worn on it. The classical readings preserve both, and neither changes the point.

keyTerms.gloss: We deliver you, bring you clear
keyTerms.note: The same verb used across the Quran for rescuing believers from destruction. Applying it to a corpse is deliberately jarring, since what is saved is the shell rather than the person.
The word used for verses of scripture and for features of the world. Making a human body one places a person's end in the same category as a sunrise, something set out to be read.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian landscape kept its ruins. Carved facades, broken dams and abandoned wells stood along the routes, and travellers passed them without stopping. The Quran repeatedly points at such places and then remarks on how few people look. This ayah adds a body to that list of unread evidence, and finishes with the same observation about human attention.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere says this ruler was seized as an example for the last and the first. In another place it says such peoples were made a precedent and an example for those who came after. Being turned into a lesson is a recurring fate in the text. This is the only place where a preserved body is named as the means of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A striking claim is made and then quietly undercut. Physical evidence is left for later generations. The very next clause says most people pay no heed to signs. That repeats the long argument of this surah, that evidence does not compel. The passage also makes a point about what survives a person. Everything the man was is gone. What remains is a lesson for other people, which is not the kind of permanence anyone seeks.

crossReferences.why: Says the same ruler was seized as an exemplary punishment, for the last and the first.
States that they were made a precedent and an example for those who came afterwards.
Repeats this ayah's closing point a few verses later, that signs avail nothing without belief.

studies.applyIt: Think of one story from your own family that gets told as a warning. Someone's choices, a business that failed, a rift nobody repaired. Notice that being a lesson for others was not what that person wanted. Then ask, without drama, what you are currently doing that could be told that way, and whether it is worth it.
studies.explainEasier: God told the king it was too late, because he had refused for so long. But God said his body would be kept safe, so that later people could see it as a sign. Most people take no notice of signs.

studies.title: They Differed After Knowledge
studies.meaning: Deliverance is followed by settlement in a place described as honourable, and by good provision. Then the sentence turns. They did not fall into disagreement until knowledge reached them. Early scholars read this as the striking part. Division came after clarity arrived, not before it, which rules out confusion as the cause. The closing clause hands the whole dispute to a judgement none of the parties will conduct, on a day when the matter is settled rather than argued.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the story section of the surah. Passages elsewhere in the Quran give the same sequence for the same community. They add scripture, wisdom and prophecy to the gifts, and name rivalry as the cause of the split. The audience being addressed was itself dividing over a message. The point of the account is the pattern rather than the particular history.

keyTerms.note: The verb for assigning someone a place to live, sharing its root with the word for taking up residence used earlier in this surah. It describes an allotment made rather than a territory seized.
The word for truthfulness attached to a dwelling place, an idiom for something genuine and well-founded. The Quran uses similar constructions elsewhere for a firm footing and a sound entry.

keyTerms.gloss: they differed, fell out of step
keyTerms.note: From a root for coming after and taking turns, so difference is pictured as people no longer moving together. The same verb was used near the surah's start for humanity as a whole.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal communities in Arabia split most often at their strongest, not their weakest. A clan under threat held together.
