Quarrels over rank, water rights and inheritance surfaced once the pressure lifted and there was something worth arguing about. Everyone in that audience had watched a family divide after a windfall. The sequence this ayah describes was a familiar shape of prosperity, not a strange one.
studies.didYouKnow: Another surah gives this same history with more detail. It lists the Book, wisdom and prophecy among the gifts. Then it names the cause of the division outright: rivalry among themselves, not any lack of clarity. The opening of this surah also used the same verb for the whole human race. So the pattern is stated twice, once for everyone and once for one people.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge is shown to be able to divide people rather than unite them. That is an uncomfortable thing to observe about religious communities. The cause named elsewhere is rivalry. So what splits a group is not what they know but what they do with the standing it gives them. Handing judgement to God then removes the assumption that the winning side in such a dispute has been proved right.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller version of the same history and names rivalry as the cause of the split.
States the same pattern at the scale of all humanity, near the beginning of this surah.
Describes division breaking out among those who received the scripture, after the proofs came.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement inside a group you belong to where both sides know the sources well. Ask what the argument is actually protecting: a reading, or a position. You can usually tell by noticing whether new information ever changes anyone's mind. Then decide which of those two you are defending this week.
studies.explainEasier: God gave the Children of Israel a good place to live and good things to eat. They only began to argue once they had been given real knowledge. God will settle their arguments on the last day.

studies.title: Ask Those Who Read Before
studies.meaning: A conditional is set up, and the classical scholars handle it with care. Most read the doubt as not applying at all. Arabic uses this construction to address a supposition rather than assert it. Reports are passed down of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) saying he neither doubted nor asked. Others take the address as reaching past him to any listener in doubt. What the ayah then does is remarkable in either reading. It points doubt outward, toward people who held earlier scripture, rather than telling it to be quiet.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Jewish and Christian communities were present in Arabia and along the trade routes north and south, and their scholars were known as people who possessed books. Elsewhere the Quran calls it a sign that the learned among the Children of Israel recognised the message, and records a witness from among them who testified and believed. Those passages give this instruction its practical sense.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be pierced or joined at two edges, so doubt is pictured as being stuck between two things. It names a divided state rather than disbelief, which is why the response offered is enquiry.
A plain imperative to ask a question of someone else. Nothing softens it, and the ayah does not qualify whom to trust, which is why the commentators discuss at length who exactly is being addressed.

From a root for pulling at something from two sides, as when milking or disputing. It describes people held in contention rather than settled opponents, which keeps the warning within the subject of doubt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge in Arabia moved by asking. There were few books and almost no schools. A question about lineage went to the tribal genealogist. A question about stars went to a navigator. A question about earlier scripture went to whoever had met people who owned it. Going to a person who knows was the normal shape of enquiry, and travelling merchants met such people every season.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names those who read earlier scripture in several places as witnesses rather than as rivals. One passage calls it a sign that the scholars among the Children of Israel recognised this message. Another records a witness from among them who testified to its like and believed. Those verses sit in different surahs from very different periods.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Doubt is treated as a question with somewhere to go, not as a fault to be crushed. That is the most striking move in the passage. The instruction is to look into it, not to try harder at believing. It also assumes the revelations are continuous, strongly enough to make earlier readers useful witnesses. The warning that follows is about settling into wavering, not about having the doubt at all.

crossReferences.why: Calls it a sign that the scholars of the Children of Israel recognised this message.
Records a witness from among them who testified to its like and believed, while others turned away.
States earlier in this surah that the Quran confirms what came before it, which this instruction assumes.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you privately doubt and treat it as a question rather than a fault. Write it down in a single sentence, then find a person or a book that has actually thought about it. Most unexamined doubts survive on being unspoken, and this ayah's response to uncertainty is not silence but enquiry.
studies.explainEasier: If you are unsure about what God has sent down, the verse says to ask the people who read the earlier books. The truth has come from your Lord. So do not stay stuck among the people who keep wavering.

studies.title: Even If Every Sign Came
studies.meaning: Three short verses tighten step by step. First a warning against joining those who deny the signs. Then a statement about people the word has already settled upon. Then the limit case. Even if every sign arrived, they would not believe, until the painful punishment is in front of them. Early scholars are careful that the sequence describes a settled refusal, not an imposed one. The surah said a few verses earlier that people wrong only themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It follows the account of Moses and closes the argument of the surah about evidence. Demands for signs run through the whole surah. They start with the request for a miracle in its early pages and go on to the challenge to produce a chapter. This passage states the outcome of that argument: the demand was never really about evidence.

keyTerms.gloss: the losers, those at a loss
keyTerms.note: From the vocabulary of trade, describing a merchant whose capital has gone. It frames denial as a bad transaction rather than as an offence, which is a strikingly commercial way to name it.
From the root for what is real and what is owed. Applied to a word it means the sentence has become due, so what is described is a debt maturing rather than a decree issued.
The most complete form the demand could take, since the objectors had been asking for particular signs. Granting all of them hypothetically shows the request was not the actual obstacle.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bargaining in the Meccan markets often had nothing to do with price. A buyer who did not mean to purchase could raise objection after objection. Traders learned to spot the pattern quickly, since each answered objection produced a new one. Everyone in that audience knew the difference between a customer who needed convincing and one who was never going to buy.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran presses this point to its limit in more than one place. One passage says that even if angels came down and the dead spoke to them, they still would not believe. Another does it in a surah that opens with these same three letters. It imagines a gate opened in the sky and the objectors climbing through it, only to say their eyes have been bewitched.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage completes an argument the surah has built since its opening pages. Evidence does not compel, and asking for more of it can be a way of never deciding. Naming the outcome as loss rather than punishment keeps the weight on the account of the person. The warning at the start is addressed to the one delivering the message. Even the messenger is being told where the line runs.

crossReferences.why: Presses the same hypothetical further, angels sent down and the dead speaking, with no change.
Imagines a gate opened in the sky and the objectors saying their eyes have been bewitched.
Records the original demand for a sign earlier in this surah, answered by placing it with God.

studies.applyIt: Notice an argument where you keep asking for more information and never act on what arrives. A decision at work, a change in your health, something someone told you clearly. Ask what evidence would actually move you, and write it down. If you cannot name any, you have learned something more useful than the answer.
studies.explainEasier: The verse warns against calling the signs of God lies, because that ends in loss. Some people have made up their minds for good. They would not believe even if every sign came to them. They only stop when the pain arrives.

studies.title: Except The People Of Jonah
studies.meaning: A regret is expressed about towns whose belief came too late to help them. Then one exception is named. The people of Jonah believed, the disgrace hanging over them was lifted, and they were given time. Early scholars note that this is the only case in the Quran of a community turning together at the last moment and being spared. That is what makes the wording so careful. What is removed is named as the suffering of disgrace in this life. What is granted is a term, not a guarantee.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah carries this prophet's name and this is the only ayah in it that mentions him, and the only mention of his people anywhere in the Quran outside a brief account in another surah. Nothing here retells his story. The surah assumes the audience knows enough of it for the exception to register, and uses only the outcome.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something proving useful, in the past tense with a negative framing before it. It states the ordinary rule by regretting its absence, which makes the exception that follows sharper.
From a root for shame that others can see. What was lifted is named as this rather than as punishment in general, so the specific relief was to their standing among the living.

keyTerms.gloss: for a time, until a term
keyTerms.note: An indefinite period with an end implied but unstated. It qualifies the reprieve honestly, granting comfort without pretending the community had been given something permanent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian communities decided things as a group. A tribe took or refused a treaty together. Single people rarely broke from a stand their elders had taken, since safety came from the group. A whole town turning at once was a familiar event, not a strange one. It needed the leaders to move. That is exactly what did not happen in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in this surah that names Jonah, though the surah carries his name. Another surah tells the rest of his story. It gives the size of the people he was sent to as a hundred thousand or more. It adds that they believed and were given enjoyment for a while, using the same root this ayah ends on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An exception is recorded rather than a rule revised. The passage holds two things together. Belief that arrives with the punishment in view does not normally help. Yet one community was spared. That leaves the door open without making it a plan anyone can count on. It also puts the difference in a whole people moving together, which is harder and rarer than one person changing his mind.

crossReferences.why: Tells the rest of this prophet's story and gives the number of those who believed.
Records his cry from the darkness and the deliverance that followed it.
Gives the counter-case earlier in this surah, a late declaration that was not accepted.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change your household or team needs that no one person can make alone. Everyone is waiting for someone else to move. Be the one who names it out loud this week, without accusing anybody. Collective turns start with a single person saying the thing everyone already knows, and that is the whole distance in this ayah.
studies.explainEasier: No town ever believed in time for it to help them. The people of Jonah were the one exception. When they believed, God lifted the shame that was about to fall on them and let them live on for a while.

studies.title: Will You Compel People
studies.meaning: A statement and a question. God could have brought everyone on earth to belief, and did not; so are you going to force people until they believe. Early scholars read the question as addressed to a man worn out by the effort of persuading, not to anyone considering force. The second verse gives the reason: no soul believes except by the leave of God. Belief is placed beyond the reach of pressure, which makes the exhaustion misplaced rather than the effort wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has argued its case from every direction and recorded the refusal each time. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had spent years on people he had known all his life. This question arrives where the surah has finished its argument. It is aimed at the one making it, not at the audience.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what is hated or imposed against inclination. Its use in a question makes the whole idea sound absurd, since what would be produced by force is not the thing being sought.
The root is the ear, so permission is pictured as something heard from the one entitled to give it. The surah used the same word earlier for intercession, placing both under the same authority.
The root describes the hobble that keeps a camel from wandering off. Reason in this word is a restraint that holds a person in place, so its absence is drift rather than stupidity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Conversion in Arabia normally moved through tribes rather than single people. When a chief accepted something, his people generally followed. Pressure applied at the top was the usual way to change a community. Everyone understood how that worked. Everyone had also seen positions taken up for convenience and dropped just as easily. The question in this ayah refuses a method its first hearers would have thought quite practical.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states this limit in several places and in different tones. One passage says the truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve. Another tells the Prophet he was not appointed a guardian or a manager over people. The best known of them declares plainly that there is no compulsion in religion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is described as something only God grants. That cuts two ways at once. It lifts an impossible responsibility off the messenger. It also removes any warrant for pressure, since force cannot produce what is being asked for. The passage leaves a real tension open. It holds the leave of God and human responsibility together without explaining the join, and the classical tradition keeps that tension rather than dissolving it.

crossReferences.why: States the principle directly, that there is no compulsion in religion, the way having become clear.
Puts the choice in the plainest terms, whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may not.
Says the same thing about God's will and denies that the messenger is a guardian over them.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have been working on. A child, a sibling, a friend whose choices worry you. Count how many conversations you have had about it. Then leave it alone for a month and keep the relationship instead. The ayah is addressed to someone doing exactly what you are doing, and its answer is that the outcome was never on your side of the line.
studies.explainEasier: If God had wanted it, everyone on earth would have believed. He did not make that happen. So no one can push another person into believing. Belief only comes when God allows it to.

studies.title: Look At What Is There
studies.meaning: An instruction and then a limit placed on it in the same breath. Look at what is in the heavens and the earth, which the early scholars read as a call to sustained observation rather than a glance. Then the qualification: signs and warnings are of no use to a people who will not believe. The two halves are not in tension. The looking is still commanded, and the ayah simply declines to promise that it works on everyone, which is the position of the surah throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing movement of the surah, after the argument has been made and refused. The surah opened by pointing at sun, moon, night and day as signs for people who know, are watchful and reflect. This ayah repeats the gesture without the qualifying clause and adds instead a statement about who it will not reach.

keyTerms.note: The verb for directing the gaze deliberately, distinct from simply seeing. It is a plural imperative addressed to everyone, which makes observation something commanded rather than recommended.
An open question word with no object supplied. Nothing is specified for the reader to find, so the instruction leaves the whole sky and earth available and does not narrow the search.
A plural that can mean both the warnings given and the people who bring them. Pairing it with signs covers the two channels the surah has used, the natural world and the messengers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Observation was a survival skill in Arabia, not a pastime. A man read the sky for rain, the ground for tracks, and the behaviour of animals for water. Children were trained in it early. Everyone in that audience was already a skilled observer. What the ayah asks for is not a new ability. It is the same attention turned toward a different question.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this instruction to look in several places. Elsewhere it pairs the looking with an unusual claim. The proofs will be shown on the horizons and within people themselves, until it becomes clear. Another passage says there are signs on earth for the convinced, and adds, within yourselves, do you not see. The looking is turned outward and inward in the same breath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that usually come apart. One is the command to look into the world. The other is the admission that looking does not settle belief. The passage does not weaken either one. It keeps observation as a real duty while denying that it works as proof. That puts the deciding factor in the observer, which fits everything the surah has said about hearing without receiving.

crossReferences.why: Promises proofs shown on the horizons and within people themselves until the truth becomes clear.
Names signs on earth for the convinced and then turns the same attention inward.
Opens this surah with the same gesture toward the heavens and the earth, for people who are watchful.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and spend five minutes looking up, without trying to feel anything. That is all the ayah asks. Look at what is there. Most of us have not done it on purpose in years. The instruction is a plain order, not a suggestion for people already drawn to it.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to look at everything in the sky and on the earth. It is all there to be seen. But signs and warnings do not help people who have already decided not to believe.

studies.title: Binding Upon Us To Save
studies.meaning: The question about what they are waiting for answers itself. Nothing but days like those of the peoples who went before. Then comes the instruction to wait, with the speaker joining them in it, exactly as earlier in the surah. The last clause carries the weight. Deliverance of the messengers and the believers is described as a duty upon God, one He has taken on Himself. Early scholars note that nothing binds God from outside. The obligation is one He has assumed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing section where the surah gathers its themes. The community being addressed was small and under pressure, with no rescue in sight. The promise is stated in the strongest grammar available, not as encouragement. Passages elsewhere use the same construction. They say that helping the believers is a duty upon God.

keyTerms.note: The plural of day, used in Arabic idiom for the notable episodes of a people, their battles and their downfalls. It names a kind of event rather than a stretch of time.

An intensive verb for pulling someone out of what is closing in, used through this surah for Noah's survivors and for the crossing of the sea. Its repetition ties the promise to cases already narrated.
The word for what is real and what is owed, placed with a preposition of obligation. Nothing external can bind God, so the phrase describes a commitment taken on rather than imposed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The days of the Arabs was a set phrase for the famous battles and reversals that tribal memory kept. Poets recited them, and people used them to settle claims about honour. Every clan knew its own days and the days of its enemies. When this ayah asks whether they expect anything but days like those of the people before them, it borrows that language exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The construction naming something as a duty upon God appears in a few places in the Quran. The object is almost always help or deliverance for the believers. One passage says it in nearly the same words, after describing earlier messengers who came with clear proofs. Another states that God will support His messengers and those who believe, both in this life and on the Day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A duty God takes on Himself is a striking way to describe a promise. It keeps His freedom, since nothing outside Him forces the matter. It also gives the promise a firmness that a mere intention would not have. That changes how a believer waits. What is offered is not a chance weighed against circumstances. It is something God has undertaken, which is why the instruction here is simply to wait rather than to calculate.

crossReferences.why: States the same duty in almost identical words, after describing earlier messengers and their proofs.
Promises support for the messengers and the believers in this life and on the Day of witnesses.
Closes the account of a prophet's rescue with the statement that thus the faithful are saved.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk about waiting for something out of your hands. Most of us phrase it as odds. It might work out, we will see. Try phrasing one thing this week as a promise someone made rather than a chance, and notice how differently the waiting sits.
studies.explainEasier: People who refuse the message are only waiting for days like the ones that came to peoples before them. God tells the messenger to wait with them. In the end God saves His messengers and the people who believe.

studies.title: If You Are In Doubt
studies.meaning: Addressed to people unsure about the religion of the speaker, the answer states what he does not do and then what he does. He does not serve what they serve. He serves the God who will end their lives. That is a pointed way to identify Him, since the one thing they cannot dispute is that dying happens. Two more instructions follow: to be among the believers, and to set his face toward the religion as one turning away from every rival. Early scholars read the sequence as a full position stated without argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of the surah. Passages elsewhere give the same instruction in almost the same order. One has the messenger say he was commanded to serve God with his religion made purely His. It adds that he fears the punishment of a great Day if he disobeys. The opening of this surah carried the same fear in nearly the same words.

keyTerms.note: From the root for paying a debt in full. Identifying God by this act rather than by creation chooses the one event in the objectors' future that none of them was prepared to argue about.
An idiom for directing yourself wholly toward something, using the verb for standing a thing upright. It describes orientation of the whole person rather than agreement with a proposition.

From a root for inclining away from something toward something else. The Quran uses it particularly of Abraham, describing a person who has turned from every rival claim without belonging to any party.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Mecca was inherited and shared. There were no words for a private position. A man belonged to the practice of his clan as he belonged to its line. A few people are remembered for stepping away from the cults of the city before the message came. They were thought odd. The culture had no ordinary place for a person who stood apart like that.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the word for turning away from rivals about a dozen times. It is attached most often to Abraham. One passage using it states that he was neither a Jew nor a Christian. Here the same word describes the stance asked of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly. An ancient description becomes a present instruction.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Doubt about a religion is answered with a description rather than a defence. Nothing is proved. The passage simply states where the speaker stands and what he refuses. Identifying God as the one who takes life does something specific too. It grounds the claim in an event nobody escapes. That makes the position hard to file away as one option among several. What is asked for is orientation, not opinion.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instructions in the same order, including the fear of a great Day if he disobeys.
Uses the identical phrase about setting the face toward the religion, turning from every rival.
Has Abraham use the same word for himself, directing his face to the One who created all.

studies.applyIt: Write one sentence saying what you actually hold, without defending it and without comparing it to anything. Most of us have never done this and find it harder than arguing. The passage answers doubt by stating a position plainly, and you cannot do that until you know what yours is in your own words.
studies.explainEasier: The messenger is told to say this to people who doubt his religion. He does not worship the things they worship. He worships the God who will one day take their lives. He was told to believe and to stay away from partners.

studies.title: What Neither Helps Nor Harms
studies.meaning: The instruction is defined by capability rather than by identity. Do not call on what cannot benefit you and cannot harm you. That is a description before it is a prohibition. Early scholars note that both halves matter. The objects can do no good, so there is nothing to gain. They can do no harm, so there is nothing to fear in leaving them. The consequence named for doing it anyway is not punishment but a category. The person would then be among the wrongdoers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing instructions of the surah. The argument about go-betweens has run through the whole chapter. It began with the question of whether God could be unaware of such an office. It ended with the statement that those invoked follow nothing but guesswork. This ayah gives the practical upshot. It is addressed in the singular, to one person, not to the objectors.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers summoning, appealing and praying, from the same root as the word for supplication. Its breadth matters, since the instruction reaches every kind of address, not only formal worship.

Practical usefulness rather than favour. The Quran repeatedly pairs it with its opposite when describing what people invoke, testing such objects by the plainest possible standard, whether anything follows.
From a root for darkness and for putting something in the wrong place. It names misplacement, so directing appeals to what cannot answer is an error of location before it is an offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear kept many practices alive more than hope did. A traveller touched a stone at a shrine on his way out of the valley not because he expected much but because omitting it felt dangerous. Everyone knew someone whose luck had turned after a neglected observance. The second half of this ayah addresses that fear directly, saying the objects cannot hurt you either.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of what cannot harm and cannot benefit runs through the Quran as a standing test. One surah uses it of what a man calls on instead of God. Another puts it as a question from Abraham to his people. A third answers it with a picture of hands stretched toward water that never reaches the mouth. The test is always practical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument closes on capability rather than on authority. The passage does not say such practices are forbidden. It says they are pointless in both directions, which meets the two motives people actually have. Naming the result as being among the wrongdoers is precise too. A misdirected appeal puts something in the wrong place. The injury falls on the one who does it, since nothing has been taken from God.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pairing and adds that the harm of such a master is nearer than any benefit.
Puts the same test as a question from Abraham to his people about what they served.
Compares such prayers to hands stretched toward water that never reaches the mouth.

studies.applyIt: Notice one small thing you do out of a vague sense that not doing it would be unlucky. A phrase, a routine, an object you keep. Ask whether you believe it can actually help, then whether you believe it can harm. Most people find the second answer is the one holding the practice in place.
studies.explainEasier: The verse says not to pray to anything besides God. Those things cannot help you, and they cannot hurt you either. If you call on them anyway, you have put yourself among the people who do wrong.

studies.title: Nothing Can Turn It Back
studies.meaning: The two halves are not built the same way, and the difference is the point. Harm is described as a touch, with its removal denied to anyone but Him. Good is described as something He intends for you, with nothing able to turn His bounty back. The second clause moves from contact to purpose, and early scholars note that the imbalance runs in favour of the good. The closing names are forgiveness and mercy rather than power.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing passage of a surah that has spent its length on people calling upon things that could neither harm nor help them. The verses before it gather the whole argument into an instruction about which way to turn. This is the final piece of that summary. Early scholars read the two divine names at the end as the surah's chosen resting point.

keyTerms.note: An agent noun from the verb to send something back. It pictures bounty as already in motion, so refusing it would mean intercepting something on its way rather than preventing a decision.

keyTerms.gloss: intends for you, wants for you
keyTerms.note: A verb of will rather than of contact. Set opposite the word for touching in the first half, it gives the good a source in intention while the harm is described only as arriving.
A general word for damage of any kind. Its indefinite form leaves the scale unspecified, so the sentence covers a minor setback and a catastrophe in exactly the same terms.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speaking to the powerful ran through go-betweens. A man in trouble found someone with standing to speak for him. A favour granted could be blocked by a rival with better access. Everyone understood that gifts could be intercepted on the way. Saying that nothing turns back this bounty described a channel with nobody standing in it, which was a strange idea in a world of brokers.
studies.didYouKnow: The first half of this verse appears almost word for word earlier in the Quran, at 6:17, but the second half differs. There the good is a touch, matching the harm; here it is something intended, and the closing divine names change along with it. The variation is small enough to vanish in translation and consistent in the Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once, and they pull in different directions unless read carefully. Nothing reaches a person outside God's decree. And nothing can block what He intends for them. The first removes the illusion of independent threats. The second removes the fear of blocked good. Ending on forgiveness and mercy rather than on might tells the reader which of the two the passage expects them to need.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement with its second half built differently, in a Meccan surah.
States that whatever mercy God opens for people, nobody can withhold it.
Asks whether the things called upon beside God could hold back His mercy.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good thing you have stopped hoping for because of who is standing in the way: a person, a system, a decision that went against you. Say the second half of this verse about that specific case. You are not predicting an outcome. You are checking whether you had quietly promoted an obstacle into a decider.
studies.explainEasier: If God lets harm reach you, only he can take it away. If he wants good for you, nobody can stop it reaching you. He is the one who forgives and the one who shows mercy.

studies.title: Be Patient Until He Judges
studies.meaning: The surah closes by dividing responsibility. The truth has arrived. From that point, guidance or straying comes back to each person alone. The one who delivered it is told plainly that he is not a guardian over anyone. Then two final instructions: follow what is revealed, and be patient until God judges. Early scholars note that patience here is given an endpoint rather than asked for without limit. The endpoint is a judgement, not a result the messenger can recognise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and these are the last two verses of the surah. The chapter has moved through creation, argument, the demands of the objectors, the accounts of Noah and Moses, and the exception of the people of Jonah. It ends with no resolution to the situation in Mecca. The instruction to wait for the judgement of God is offered instead of a promise about when.

keyTerms.note: One appointed to manage another's affairs, from the same root as the word for reliance used through this surah. Denying the role to the messenger keeps the transfer of responsibility running only upward.
From a root for binding something in place and for a bitter plant. Patience in this word is restraint under difficulty rather than calm feeling, which is why it can be commanded.
The root joins restraint and sound judgement, and gives the word applied to this Book in the surah's opening line. The chapter therefore ends on the same root it began with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Arabia ended when the arbitrator ruled. The parties waited however long that took. Nobody expected to see the outcome before the judgement, and pressing the arbitrator was itself a fault. The closing instruction uses that ordinary procedure. The case has been made. The deciding belongs elsewhere. What is left for the claimant is to hold his position without pressing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for judgement that closes this surah shares its root with the word describing the Book in its very first verse, translated there as wise. The chapter opens by calling the scripture firmly judged. It closes by handing the outcome to the best of judges. The same three letters frame the whole surah at both ends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is divided along a clear line at the end. What a person does with the truth belongs to that person. The one who delivered it holds neither credit nor blame. That protects both from a burden that is not theirs. Attaching an endpoint to patience is just as deliberate. What is asked for is not endurance without limit. It is waiting for one specific event, which is a different thing to carry.

crossReferences.why: States the same division in nearly identical words, ending with you are not their overseer.
Gives the same closing instruction, patience for the decision of your Lord, in another surah.
The opening of this surah, which uses the same root for the Book that its final word uses for judgement.

studies.applyIt: Take one situation where you have said everything you can say. Write down, in a sentence, what part of it is now genuinely not yours. Then set an actual date to revisit it rather than turning it over daily. Patience with an endpoint is a different task from patience without one, and this ayah gives it one.
studies.explainEasier: The truth has reached you from your Lord. If you follow it, that is good for you. If you go the wrong way, that harms only you. The messenger is not in charge of you, and he waits for God to judge.
